items.title: Bootstrap validation of random forest models
items.body:
A typical workflow in machine learning is to split data into train and test sets, using the former to develop a model and the latter to evaluate its ability to generalize.

Some dispute this as a best practice, advocating for an alternative approach of validation that does not split the data. Our Frank Harrell is one such advocate.

  1. Splitting the data wastes precious data that could have been used for training, so train on the entire dataset.

  2. However, then we risk overfitting. We always risk overfitting, but when we have holdout data, we can catch that we have just played connect-the-dots.

  3. Therefore, bootstrap your data, fit the model to the bootstrap sample, evaluate that model on the full data set, and see how that performance compares to the performance of the model that was trained on the entire data set. Because we do these many times with bootstrap samples, we can get a good estimate of overfitting when we trained on the entire data set.

  4. If we are happy with how little overfitting there is, then we should use the model that was trained on the entire data set, which we now consider validated.

This makes sense for training, for instance, generalized linear models, even neural networks. However, if we train a random forest, then there is already bootstrapping occurring in fitting the model. Is this bootstrap approach, then, useful for validating random forests? Would a tweak be warranted?

items.title: Probability of hitting time and additional time $X+Y$ in a diffusion process
items.body:
Let $X$ follow an inverse Gaussian distribution, and $Y\mid X$ a Gaussian distribution.

$$X \sim IG\left( \frac{\alpha}{v_X}, \frac{\alpha^2}{2D_X} \right)$$ $$Y_{\text{given $X=x$}} \sim \mathcal N(v_Y x,\ 2D_Y x). $$

with positive parameters/constants $\alpha, v_X, v_Y, D_X, D_Y$

Question/problem: Derive a simple expression for the distribution of $T = X+Y$.

I believe that an elegant expression can be made in terms of the CDF/PDF of the normal distribution, based on the situation being similar to a 2D Wiener process with drift.

(edit: after trying to work out a solution by picturing it as a 2D Wiener process with drift and an absorbing boundary, this is probably harder than I thought, and an approximation might be necessary)

Example for a similar type of derivtion or what I am looking for is in the question: Compound Poisson Distribution with sum of exponential random variables

There, a 2D random walk could be expressed as a non-central chi-squared distribution. Or alternatively, the convolution describing the compound distribution could be worked out and expressed as a Bessel function.

Possibly this expression has also a simple expression.

This question relates to a larger problem here: Probability distribution of $T=X+Y+Z$ with $Y,Z$ conditionally dependent on $X$

A motivation is that $T=X+Y$ is like a hitting time $X$, but with an additional time $Y$ that relates to the time $X$

Edit: example/explanation of the distribution by generation/simulation with some code

alpha = 1
Dx = 1
Dy = 1
vx = 1
vy = 1

n = 10^4
set.seed(1)

x = statmod::rinvgauss(n, 
                       mean = alpha/vx,
                       shape = alpha^2/2/Dx)
y = rnorm(n, 
          mean = vy*x, 
          sd = sqrt(2*Dy*x))

hist(x+y, freq = 1, breaks = 40)

Sidenote: in the original linked problem the distribution of $Y$ conditional on $X$ is actually a non-central chi-squared distribution with zero degrees of freedom.

Potentially that might help with an approach that gives a simple expression for an estimate of the distribution.

items.title: Statistical modeling with only a single data point
items.body:
The vast majority of statistical literature involves having a dataset which can be partitioned into $n$ data points, $\mathbf{x} = \{x_1,...,x_n\}$ constructing a model for the individual data partitions $p(x_i|\theta)$, and estimating parameters $\theta$ that in some way best "fit" the data, using standard approaches (e.g., Bayesian inference).

However, what if your data can't be partitioned in any meaningful way, and really needs to be treated as a single observation? Consider the following inference problem:

Given the image below, what is the speed of the car?

You might set a prior based on the typical speeds that cars in general travel at, $\pi(\theta)$, and your likelihood is probably very complex, but in principle exists. E.g., I see smoke coming from the wheels, which suggests the car is drifting, and that only happens at speeds above a certain threshold. The car also appears to be on a race track, in which cars tend to drive much faster than on normal roads.

This is a well-defined inference problem, and I could provide a point estimate of the speed of the car, or write down a posterior distribution for the speed - but how would I assess how well my model fits the data?

Many of the typical tools seem to break down here, because they very often rely on computing some expectation over the data distribution - which in this case is poorly defined. If I had a series of images of the same car taken from different angles, then sure we can recover the typical statistical framework, but in this case we don't and shouldn't need to.

What is a good way to think about how one might assess their model in this scenario?

items.title: How to quantify uncertainty for time series predictions
items.body:
I'm conducting an interrupted time series analysis to estimate the effect of an intervention.

  • I fit a (ARIMA) time series model on pre-intervention data
  • I forecast 3 months post-intervention to represent what the data might have looked like without the intervention. The reason for 3 months is because I believe the intervention is small and the impact (if at all) should only last for a short period of time. By looking at more than a 3 month post-intervention period, I suspect that other factors might influence the data and we would end up measuring their influence instead.
  • I want to compare forecasts (counterfactual) to the actual data in order to estimate the intervention effect

What I have:

  • Actuals (post-intervention): $y_1, y_2, y_3$
  • Forecasts from model: $\hat{y}_1, \hat{y}_2, \hat{y}_3$
  • 95% prediction intervals on the forecast: $[\hat{y}_i^L, \hat{y}_i^U]$ for $i = 1, 2, 3$

What I want to estimate:

  1. The average intervention effect over 3 months: $\bar{d} = \frac{1}{3} \sum_{i=1}^{3} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)$
  2. An interval quantifying the uncertainty around $\bar{d}$

I thought monte carlo might be the safest way to do this?

library(forecast)

set.seed(123)
# true intervention effect is -2
pre <- arima.sim(n = 60, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1)
post_actuals <- arima.sim(n = 3, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1) - 2

model <- auto.arima(pre)

n_sims <- 10000
simulated_paths <- replicate(n_sims, simulate(model, nsim = 3, future = TRUE))

mean_diffs <- apply(simulated_paths, 2, function(path) {
  mean(post_actuals - path)
})

> cat("Point estimate:", mean(mean_diffs), "\n")
Point estimate: -0.3069363 
> cat("95% interval:", quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975)), "\n")
95% interval: -2.09259 1.545589

Edit 1: I have updated my original approach to reflect uncertainty from model parameter estimates (still assumes auto.arima picked the correct model):

library(forecast)
library(MASS)

set.seed(123)

pre <- arima.sim(n = 60, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1)
post_actuals <- arima.sim(n = 3, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1) - 2

model <- auto.arima(pre)

coef_est <- coef(model)
vcov_mat <- vcov(model)
sigma_est <- sqrt(model$sigma2)

n_sims <- 10000
mean_diffs <- numeric(n_sims)

for (sim in 1:n_sims) {
    print(sim)
    coef_draw <- mvrnorm(n = 1, mu = coef_est, Sigma = vcov_mat)
    
    order <- arimaorder(model)
    p <- order[1]
    q <- order[3]
    
    ar_coefs <- if (p > 0) coef_draw[paste0("ar", 1:p)] else numeric(0)
    ma_coefs <- if (q > 0) coef_draw[paste0("ma", 1:q)] else numeric(0)
    intercept <- if ("intercept" %in% names(coef_draw)) coef_draw["intercept"] else 0
    
    if (p == 0 && q == 0) {
        sim_path <- rnorm(3, mean = intercept, sd = sigma_est)
    } else {
        model_spec <- list()
        if (p > 0) model_spec$ar <- ar_coefs
        if (q > 0) model_spec$ma <- ma_coefs
        
        sim_path <- tryCatch(
            arima.sim(n = 3, model = model_spec, sd = sigma_est) + intercept,
            error = function(e) rnorm(3, mean = intercept, sd = sigma_est)
        )
    }
    
    mean_diffs[sim] <- mean(post_actuals - sim_path)
}

It looks like the width of uncertainty has now increased (as expected) and the point estimate itself is also much different:

> cat("Point estimate:", mean(mean_diffs), "\n")
Point estimate: -0.8880676 
> cat("95% interval:", quantile(mean_diffs, c(0.025, 0.975)), "\n")
95% interval: -3.495714 1.663653

Edit 2: General outline of Stephen's procedure ("So if you do want to run with a more complex approach than the simplest one I outlined at the top, here is what I would do"). I am a bit confused and I see two different interpretations.

Interpretation 1:

  1. Define candidate models: List out ARIMA orders you want to consider

  2. Fit each candidate to full data (pre + post) with intervention as xreg (1 during intervention and 0 elsewhere)

  3. Record from each fit:

    • AICc
    • Coefficient estimates (including intervention effect)
    • Variance-covariance matrix

  4. Calculate AICc weights (uncertain how)

  5. Randomly pick one model using the weights as probabilities

  6. Randomly draw parameter values from that model's estimates and variance-covariance matrix (assuming multivariate normal)

  7. Extract the intervention effect from the drawn parameters

  8. Record it

  9. After all simulations: Look at the distribution of intervention effects —this gives a confidence interval that accounts for:

    • Model selection uncertainty (step 5)
    • Parameter estimation uncertainty (step 6)

Interpretation 2:

  1. Define candidate ARIMA models

  2. Fit each candidate to full data (pre + post) with intervention as xreg (1 during intervention and 0 elsewhere)

  3. Record from each fit: AICc, coefficient estimates, variance-covariance matrix

  4. Calculate AICc weights (uncertain how)

  5. Randomly pick a model using AICc weights

  6. Randomly draw parameters from that model's estimates and variance-covariance matrix

  7. Simulate a fake pre-intervention series using those drawn parameters

  8. Fit an ARIMA to that fake series (using auto.arima—may pick different order)

  9. Forecast forward from the model fitted in step 8

  10. Simulate fake post-intervention data by adding the drawn intervention effect to the forecast

  11. Compute effect as mean(fake post) - mean(forecast) ... which just equals the drawn intervention effect?

  12. After all simulations : Look at distribution of effects

R code for interpretation 1:

library(forecast)
library(MASS)

set.seed(123)

# Generate data
n_pre <- 60
n_post <- 3
true_effect <- -2

pre <- arima.sim(n = n_pre, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1)
post <- arima.sim(n = n_post, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1) + true_effect

full_series <- ts(c(pre, post))
intervention <- c(rep(0, n_pre), rep(1, n_post))

# Step 1: Define candidate models
candidate_orders <- list(
  c(0, 0, 0),
  c(1, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 1),
  c(1, 0, 1),
  c(2, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 2)
)

# Step 2-3: Fit each candidate, record AICc, coefs, vcov
fits <- list()
for (i in seq_along(candidate_orders)) {
  order <- candidate_orders[[i]]
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(full_series, order = order, xreg = intervention),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(fit)) {
    fits[[length(fits) + 1]] <- list(
      order = order,
      aicc = fit$aicc,
      coef = coef(fit),
      vcov = vcov(fit)
    )
  }
}

# Step 4: Calculate AICc weights
aiccs <- sapply(fits, function(x) x$aicc)
delta_aicc <- aiccs - min(aiccs)
weights <- exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc))

cat("Model weights:\n")
for (i in seq_along(fits)) {
  cat(sprintf("  ARIMA(%d,%d,%d): %.3f\n", 
              fits[[i]]$order[1], fits[[i]]$order[2], fits[[i]]$order[3], 
              weights[i]))
}

# Steps 5-8: Monte Carlo
n_sims <- 1000
effects <- numeric(n_sims)

for (sim in 1:n_sims) {
  
  if (sim %% 100 == 0) print(paste("Simulation:", sim))
  
  # Step 5: Pick a model
  model_idx <- sample(seq_along(fits), size = 1, prob = weights)
  chosen <- fits[[model_idx]]
  
  # Step 6: Draw parameters
  coef_draw <- mvrnorm(n = 1, mu = chosen$coef, Sigma = chosen$vcov)
  
  # Step 7: Extract intervention effect
  effects[sim] <- coef_draw["xreg"]
}

# Step 8: Results
cat("\n=== INTERPRETATION 1 RESULTS ===\n")
cat("True effect:", true_effect, "\n")
cat("Point estimate:", mean(effects), "\n")
cat("95% interval:", quantile(effects, c(0.025, 0.975)), "\n")

R code for interpretation 2:

library(forecast)
library(MASS)
set.seed(123)

# Generate data
n_pre <- 60
n_post <- 3
true_effect <- -2

pre <- arima.sim(n = n_pre, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1)
post <- arima.sim(n = n_post, model = list(ar = 0.7, ma = 0.2), sd = 1) + true_effect

full_series <- ts(c(pre, post))
intervention <- c(rep(0, n_pre), rep(1, n_post))

# Step 1: Define candidate models
candidate_orders <- list(
  c(0, 0, 0),
  c(1, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 1),
  c(1, 0, 1),
  c(2, 0, 0),
  c(0, 0, 2)
)

# Step 2-3: Fit each candidate, record AICc, coefs, vcov
fits <- list()
for (i in seq_along(candidate_orders)) {
  order <- candidate_orders[[i]]
  fit <- tryCatch(
    Arima(full_series, order = order, xreg = intervention),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(fit)) {
    fits[[length(fits) + 1]] <- list(
      order = order,
      aicc = fit$aicc,
      coef = coef(fit),
      vcov = vcov(fit)
    )
  }
}

# Step 4: Calculate AICc weights
aiccs <- sapply(fits, function(x) x$aicc)
delta_aicc <- aiccs - min(aiccs)
weights <- exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc))

cat("Model weights:\n")
for (i in seq_along(fits)) {
  cat(sprintf("  ARIMA(%d,%d,%d): %.3f\n", 
              fits[[i]]$order[1], fits[[i]]$order[2], fits[[i]]$order[3], 
              weights[i]))
}

# Steps 5-11: Monte Carlo
n_sims <- 1000
effects <- numeric(n_sims)

for (sim in 1:n_sims) {
  
  if (sim %% 100 == 0) print(paste("Simulation:", sim))
  
  # Step 5: Pick a model
  model_idx <- sample(seq_along(fits), size = 1, prob = weights)
  chosen <- fits[[model_idx]]
  
  # Step 6: Draw parameters
  coef_draw <- mvrnorm(n = 1, mu = chosen$coef, Sigma = chosen$vcov)
  
  order <- chosen$order
  p <- order[1]
  q <- order[3]
  
  ar_coefs <- if (p > 0) coef_draw[paste0("ar", 1:p)] else numeric(0)
  ma_coefs <- if (q > 0) coef_draw[paste0("ma", 1:q)] else numeric(0)
  intercept <- if ("intercept" %in% names(coef_draw)) coef_draw["intercept"] else 0
  intervention_effect <- coef_draw["xreg"]
  
  # Step 7: Simulate fake pre-intervention series
  if (p == 0 && q == 0) {
    fake_pre <- rnorm(n_pre, mean = intercept, sd = 1)
  } else {
    model_spec <- list()
    if (p > 0) model_spec$ar <- ar_coefs
    if (q > 0) model_spec$ma <- ma_coefs
    
    fake_pre <- tryCatch(
      arima.sim(n = n_pre, model = model_spec, sd = 1) + intercept,
      error = function(e) rnorm(n_pre, mean = intercept, sd = 1)
    )
  }
  
  # Step 8: Fit ARIMA to fake pre-intervention series
  fit_fake <- auto.arima(fake_pre, stepwise = TRUE, approximation = TRUE)
  
  # Step 9: Forecast forward
  fc <- forecast(fit_fake, h = n_post)
  counterfactual <- as.numeric(fc$mean)
  
  # Step 10: Fake post = forecast + intervention effect
  fake_post <- counterfactual + intervention_effect
  
  # Step 11: Effect = mean(fake_post) - mean(counterfactual)
  effects[sim] <- mean(fake_post) - mean(counterfactual)
}

# Step 12: Results
cat("\n=== INTERPRETATION 2 RESULTS ===\n")
cat("True effect:", true_effect, "\n")
cat("Point estimate:", mean(effects), "\n")
cat("95% interval:", quantile(effects, c(0.025, 0.975)), "\n")

items.title: What posterior for exponential distribution with uniform prior?
items.body:
Suppose I have the PDF of an exponential distribution which $\lambda$ parameter is unknown: $$f(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda \, e^{-\lambda x} \quad \lambda>0 \quad \text{support} = \mathbb{R_+^*}$$ Suppose I have no previous information on the parameter, so I choose a uniform prior of constant value $1$: $$\pi(\lambda) = \mathbb{1}_\mathbb{R_+} = 1$$ Thus: $$\pi(\lambda) \, f(x\mid\lambda) = \lambda \, e^{-\lambda x}$$ Now, I integrate: $$\int_{\Lambda=[0,\infty]}=\int_0^\infty \lambda \, e^{-\lambda x} \, d\lambda$$ Interrogating WolframAlpha, I get: $$\int_0^b \lambda \, e^{-\lambda x} \, d\lambda = \frac{1-e^{-bx}(bx+1)}{x^2}$$ From that, I infer: $$\int_0^ \infty \lambda \, e^{-\lambda x} \, d\lambda = \frac{1}{x^2}$$ And then the posterior: $$ \pi(\lambda \mid x) = \frac{\lambda \, e^{-\lambda x}}{\frac{1}{x^2}} = x^2 \lambda \, e^{-\lambda x} $$ $1^\text{st}$ question: am I reasoning correctly ? or please point to any incorrectness I am unhappily unaware of...

$2^\text{nd}$ question: does this posterior distribution have a specific name?

items.title: How should I compare two survival prediction models when a predictor’s definition drifts over time?
items.body:
I am comparing two survival prediction models for CNS tumor patients, and my main concern is temporal drift in histology definitions rather than ordinary overfitting.

My development dataset is SEER (diagnoses from 2000–2022), and I also have a separate external test dataset from another country. The issue is that after 2018, integrated molecular diagnosis changed part of the astrocytoma / oligodendroglioma boundary, so the meaning of some histology labels is not fully stable across time.

I am currently fitting an ordinal survival model in rms::orm() using a censored ordinal outcome created with Ocens(...). The model includes sex, topology, histology class, age spline terms, treatment variables, and several manually specified interactions specifically between histology and treatment and others. I use rcorr.cens() for discrimination, calibrate() / validate() for internal assessment, and val.surv() for external calibration at fixed time points.

In a separate workflow, I also fit a flexible parametric survival model using flexsurvspline().

My Problem

Because of the above described inconsistencies I think one need to take the temporal differences into account. So I need to somehow compare these two model:

  • Model A: era-agnostic model
  • Model B: same model, but with a post-2018 era term and selected era × histology interactions for the unstable histology boundary

Should I use some kind of cross-validation / resampling strategy using post-2018 data as held out for model comparison?

Or should I fit both models on the full development dataset and then just check how they perform on the 2018–2022 subset?

I do not want to throw away the older SEER data if it still contains useful prognostic information, but I also do not want to pretend that pre-2018 and post-2018 histology labels are perfectly exchangeable.

I would appreciate methodological advice on how to set up the comparison between A and B in a statistically defensible way.

Aside from my current situation I think this is a general problem regarding the changes that occur on data with time and their correct modeling for diagnostic/prediction purposes.

items.title: Sampling from a “transpose” multinomial?
items.body:
Consider the following process. We have $m$ balls that we wish to toss into $n$ identical urns. Each ball is tossed uniformly and independently from the others. The number of items that land in each ball is then modeled by a multinomial distribution.

What I’m interested in is not the number of balls in each urn, but the frequency vector $(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m)$ where $x_i$ denotes the number of urns with exactly $i$ balls in them. Thus $x_0$ counts the number of urns containing zero balls, $x_1$ the number of urns containing one ball, etc.

I’m not familiar with this distribution. Does it have a name? Is there an efficient algorithm for sampling from it? For reference, the value of $m$ is expected to be large (on the order of $10^{15}$, and $n$ is likely to be on the order of $m \over \ln m$ but can range anywhere from 1 to $m\text.$ Thus sampling from a multinomial distribution and summing the frequencies manually is prohibitive.

(Some context: I'm looking at an alternative to Algorithm 6 from the paper On the Generation of Random Binary Search Trees by Devroye and Robson. That algorithm works by keeping track of the number of external nodes in a binary search tree at each level in the tree, then using a multinomial sample to determine the number of nodes that will be inserted below each of those external nodes within a given timeframe. They use a Yule process as the underlying model, which makes each node's child count i.i.d. variables. I'm looking at whether it would be possible to instead start with the assumption that the number of children of each node is not i.i.d. and instead multinomially-distributed, in which case I would need to be able to determine the relative frequencies of subtree sizes. I therefore need to be able to sample exactly from the distribution, rather than getting something that's asymptotically correct.)

items.title: Statistical inference and visualization with n = 3 biological replicates
items.body:
I am currently measuring protein expression in two independent cell lines. For each cell line, there are 3 independent biological replicates. There are 20 technical replicates (aka. repeated measurements) for each biological replicate.

My understanding is that the technical replicates are not independent observations, so treating all 60 measurements per cell line as independent samples would lead to pseudoreplication. Therefore, I am planning to average the 20 technical replicates within each biological replicate, leaving me with 3 observations per cell line.

I have two questions:

  1. Is it statistically appropriate to perform an independent-samples t-test (or Welch's t-test) on the biological replicate means when there are only n = 3 biological replicates per group? Some sources seem to suggest this is acceptable, while others discourage the use of statistical tests for n = 3. Hence, I am unsure whether this method is valid, especially in the context of biostatistics.

  2. For visualisation, would it be misleading to plot all technical replicates in a violin plot while overlaying only the 3 biological replicate means as points? My concern is that the violin shape would be driven largely by technical variation (60 observations per cell line), whereas the statistical inference is based on only 3 biological replicates per cell line. I have also considered using superplots, but in my case they become visually cluttered due to the large number of technical replicates.

items.title: References on near non-identifiability
items.body:
I'm looking for references on a sort of "near non-identifiability" -- I don't know what names it might have been studied under, which makes it hard to search.

Consider the model for binary $Y$ given by $$g(P[Y=1|X,b])=\beta_0+\beta_1X+ b$$ with $b\sim N(0,\tau^2)$ and with $g()$ a link function.

If $X$ is binary we have a saturated model and it is not identifiable: it uses three parameters to specify two means and there is no information in the data apart from those means.

If $X$ is a numeric variable the model is non-identifiable when $g$ is the probit link: the model can be written as $$Y=I\{\beta_0+\beta_1x+b+\epsilon>0\}=I\{\beta_0+\beta_1x> N(0,\tau^2+1)\}$$ where $\epsilon\sim N(0,1)$. If we change $\tau$ to $\tilde\tau$ we just need to rescale the $\beta$s by $\sqrt{(\tilde\tau^2+1)/(\tau^2+1)}$ to get the same distributions for $Y$.

The model is, however, identifiable when $g$ is the logit link (with high probability at large enough sample sizes, at least).

Since logit and probit models are quite good substitutes for each other, the identifiability under the logit link has to be quite tenous. It comes from the model's specification that the relationship is exactly linear on the logit scale; varying the parameters will make the relationship slightly non-linear. I would not want to rely on estimating three parameters in this model.

For another example of this phenomenon: competing risks are identifiable under proportional hazards in a somewhat similar way

An obvious challenge is there's a spectrum of degrees of identifiability. For any model with a smooth parametrisation there are trivially going to be distinct parameter values giving distributions that are quite close. I still think there's a thing here.

So, I'm looking for literature on models that are

  • weakly identifiable
  • structurally similar to some non-identifiable model
  • in some sense, identifiable because of an assumption that we would not normally expect to hold exactly, such as linearity or additivity or proportional hazards

I'm hoping to be able to find or derive a result along the lines of: "the model stops being identifiable when we go from linear in $x$ to 'nearly linear' in $x$" with nearly linear defined perhaps in terms of contiguity or perhaps in some explicit small model. However, any leads on the study of this sort of problem would be welcome. I

items.title: After using software to perform a Mann-Whitney U test, is there any reason to report/use the normal approximation?
items.body:
My question is not about when the normal approximation is reasonable to use. There's clear guidance about that. When software provides both the exact and the approximate test, is there any reason not to just use or report the results of the exact test?

For context, I'm a professor. I'm just considering whether, for applied courses, there's any point in still teaching things like: if both ns are below 10 do the exact test. I'm all for dumping whatever chaff I can and just keeping the wheat.

Thoughts?

items.title: Sampling from a “transpose” multinomial?
items.body:
Consider the following process. We have $m$ balls that we wish to toss into $n$ identical urns. Each ball is tossed uniformly and independently from the others. The number of items that land in each ball is then modeled by a multinomial distribution.

What I’m interested in is not the number of balls in each urn, but the frequency vector $(x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m)$ where $x_i$ denotes the number of urns with exactly $i$ balls in them. Thus $x_0$ counts the number of urns containing zero balls, $x_1$ the number of urns containing one ball, etc.

I’m not familiar with this distribution. Does it have a name? Is there an efficient algorithm for sampling from it? For reference, the value of $m$ is expected to be large (on the order of $10^{15}$, and $n$ is likely to be on the order of $m \over \ln m$ but can range anywhere from 1 to $m\text.$ Thus sampling from a multinomial distribution and summing the frequencies manually is prohibitive.

(Some context: I'm looking at an alternative to Algorithm 6 from the paper On the Generation of Random Binary Search Trees by Devroye and Robson. That algorithm works by keeping track of the number of external nodes in a binary search tree at each level in the tree, then using a multinomial sample to determine the number of nodes that will be inserted below each of those external nodes within a given timeframe. They use a Yule process as the underlying model, which makes each node's child count i.i.d. variables. I'm looking at whether it would be possible to instead start with the assumption that the number of children of each node is not i.i.d. and instead multinomially-distributed, in which case I would need to be able to determine the relative frequencies of subtree sizes. I therefore need to be able to sample exactly from the distribution, rather than getting something that's asymptotically correct.)

items.title: Should the homoscedasticity and normality assumptions of linear regression be abandoned?
items.body:
In introductory statistics classes, I learned the 4 assumptions of linear regression:

  1. linearity between response and covariate
  2. independence of residuals
  3. homoscedasticity (constant variance)
  4. normality of residuals

However, I hear very strong objections from some people about the last two assumptions. They think

A. robust standard errors can deal with heteroskedasticity.

B. asymptotic theory allows you to perform valid hypothesis tests and construct confidence intervals in large samples even if the residuals are non-normal.

They think it's a disservice to still teach students the four basic assumptions.

What extra value do assumptions 3 and 4 provide that A and B do NOT provide? If that extra value is minimal, should we abandon those assumptions?

items.title: Weekly demand forecasting: Should I train on weekly or daily data and then aggregate?
items.body:
I'm currently working on a demand forecasting problem for inventory replenishment, and I'd love to hear how others would approach it.

The business requests a forecast for the next 4 weeks of stock consumption around the middle of the previous month. For example, in mid-June, I need to forecast the weekly demand for July. The challenge is that, at the time the forecast is generated, transactions from the second half of June are not yet available, creating a gap between the latest observed data and the beginning of the forecast horizon.

The data I have consists of purchase order transactions at the SKU level, including timestamp (date and time) and quantity consumed.

My main question is about the appropriate time granularity for training the forecasting model:

Option 1: Aggregate the data by SKU and ISO YearWeek, resulting in one observation per SKU per week, and train a model to directly predict the next 4 weeks.

Option 2: Keep the data at the daily level, train a model to forecast daily demand, and then aggregate the daily predictions into ISO YearWeeks to obtain the required weekly forecasts.

One additional detail is that the forecast is reported using ISO YearWeeks. As a result, some weeks within a calendar month may contain only 3 or 4 days of that month (e.g., at the beginning or end of the month), while others contain all 7 days.

My question is: Which approach would you choose, and why?

Is it generally better to train the model at the same frequency as the business target (weekly), or to preserve the daily granularity and aggregate the predictions afterward?

I'd especially appreciate hearing from anyone who has worked on similar forecasting problems in inventory planning or supply chain.

items.title: Can I consider the distribution of all the regression coefficient estimates, independent of their p-values?
items.body:
I am calculating a general linear model y=k1.*x1+k2.*x2+k3.*x3 for each subject of an experiment.

I want to study the distribution of the regression coefficient estimates corresponding to a covariate of the model, let's say the distribution of k1 values corresponding to all subjects.

I am using the fitlm Matlab function that returns a linear regression model fit to the input data. Hence I have a p-value associated to the regression coefficient estimate k1, for each subject.

Would it be correct to consider the distribution of all the regression coefficient estimates of all subjects or we should consider the distribution of the regression coefficient estimates that have significant p-values?

According to the one sample t-test, in case I consider all the regression coefficient estimates, I obtain a distribution whose mean is significantly different from zero (that is consistent with what I expect from theory). If instead I consider the distribution of only significant regression coefficients, I obtain a distribution whose mean is equal to zero.

Hence, would it be wrong to consider the distribution of all the regression coefficients estimates, whatever their p-values is?

ADDITIONAL INFORMATION REQUESTED:

  • what do y and x1-3 represent ?
  • which is the objective of understanding the distribution of estimated coefficients ?
  • How many samples ?

I am studying if there is a positive linear relationship between two quantitative metrics (y and x1) of brain. x2 and x3 are confounding variables that we would like to keep constant. Samples are median regional values of those metrics in the brain. So for each subject, y, x1, x2 and x3 have dimension that is 1 x number of regions. The quantitative metrics considered are parameters of models extracted from magnetic resonance imaging data.

The number of subjects is 29 whereas the number of regions is 118. Thus the general linear model is computed 29 times, with 118 samples for each subject. At the end, I have a distribution of 29 values of k1 regression coefficients.

As mentioned, the objective is to understand if there is a positive linear relationship between y and x1 in this context where samples are median regional values of parameters. The distribution of k1 coefficients considering all 29 subjects is mainly positioned towards positive values, so this would let me conclude that yes there is. However I don't know if it is fair, because considering only k1 regression coefficients whose p-value is lower than 0.05, the k1 regression coefficients distribution is closer to zero values. Would this mean that I should throw away the hypothesis of a positive linear relationship between y and x1 across brain regions?

items.title: Trouble with the definition of p-value
items.body:
I'm following a statistics course and our professor gave us a definition of p-value I'm having some trouble understanding. First, some preliminary notations I want to set:

  • $\Omega = A \cup A^\complement$, $A$ the rejection region
  • given a statistic $T = t(X)$, if one has $A = (T \in \Gamma)$ for some $\Gamma \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ then one calls $C = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n | t(x) \in \Gamma\}$ the rejection region for the statistic $T$.
  • $\delta$ is the decision function with respect to the reject region $C$, i.e. the indicator function of $C$. In the following we will refer to the test with $C$ or with $\delta$

At this point our professor states that a test has level of significance $\alpha$ if one has $\alpha = \text{sup}_{\theta \in \Theta_0} P_{\theta}(X \in C)$ and this definition is quite clear to me as it fits the idea of error of the first type.

The part I have some problems with is the following: given a test $\delta$ and a realization $x$ of $X$, we define the p-value as $p_{\delta}(x) = \text{inf}\{\alpha \in (0,1) | \delta(x) = 1\}$. My confusion here ensues from the fact that I don't see what the dependence of $\delta$ is wrt $\alpha$, in the following sense: as far as I understood what is going on, what one does is fix a rejection region $C$ and the moment our realization ends up in $C$ (i.e. $\delta(x) = 1$) one rejects the null hypothesis $\theta \in \Theta_0$. This however doesn't really seem to have anything to do with $\alpha$, which is a measure of what is the probability of doing an error of the first type given the rejection region I've already chosen. Hence it seems to me that $\alpha$ is dependent on $C$ (and by extension on $\delta$) and not the other way around. However in the definition it seems that once you have fixed a test $\delta$, you can move $\alpha$ around (and then if you want $p_{\delta}(x)$ just take the inf among these $\alpha$).

To sum it up, I feel like I'm missing something on this definition of p-value and would love to understand.

items.title: Why is R² not equal to the square of Pearson's correlation coefficient (r²) in my multivariate regression model?
items.body:
I'm working on calibrating air quality sensor data using a multivariate regression model (Lasso), with predictors like raw PM2.5, humidity, and temperature. After fitting the model, I compared:

R² from sklearn.metrics.r2_score(y_true, y_pred)

r from scipy.stats.pearsonr(y_true, y_pred)

Then calculated manually as :

def calculate_r2(y_true, y_pred):
    sse = ((y_true - y_pred) ** 2).sum()
    sst = ((y_true - y_true.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    r2 = 1 - (sse / sst)
    return r2

`

I noticed that R² and r² are close, but not exactly equal. For example:

R² = 0.56
r = 0.75 → r² = 0.5625

also in some case: it is r = 0.74 and R² = -2.25, here R² is negative

I understand that in simple linear regression, R² = r². But since I'm using multiple predictors, I'm wondering:

Why do R² and r² diverge (coming negative) in multivariate regression?

Is this expected behavior?

Is R² in sklearn defined differently from r²?

Under what conditions are R² and r² equal or different?

Any clarification or official source would be appreciated!

items.title: What are some examples of truly independent things that are relatable to people?
items.body:
I'm trying to come up with relatable examples to teach the concept of independence/orthogonality of two random variables $A$ and $B$. But my Bayes-Net-rotted brain keeps coming up with scenarios of how the two quantities/RVs could possibly not be independent (usually because of a common factor $C$).

Some ANTI-examples of independence:

  • Bob being $A$ (able to jump high) and Bob being $B$ (good at chess).
    • if Bob had $C$ (a good childhood with a happy family), then he is more likely to be $A$ and $B$.
  • $A$: Bob liking cats, $B$: Enrique eating a hotdog on Saturday 9/5/2026.
    • $C$: these are both dependent on the human race existing 4 billion years after the Earth's formation

I intuitively understand independence. But I'm trying to come up with a more full-proof method to explain it. Note that the explanation has to be RELATABLE. It's trivial to define mathematically.

Also, note that I understand that this question may be more philosophical, and less hard stats. I'm just trying to figure out effective analogies to teach the concept of independence/orthogonality.

items.title: Frequentist estimation but Bayesian interpretation
items.body:
Let's say that I fitted a logistic regression model to predict whether a patient has or will develop heart disease. Suppose that, for a given individual, the model estimates a 90% probability of having heart disease, and we then classify the individual as "having heart disease (1)." Let's say that the threshold is 50% (although the specific threshold is not really relevant to my question).

Correct me if I am wrong, but what we did was the following:

  1. Input the patient's features.
  2. Obtain a probability of that individual having heart disease.
  3. Interpret this probability in a Bayesian way. Since the estimated probability (90%) is above our chosen threshold, we classify the patient as having heart disease.

Is this correct?

The reason I am asking is that, from my understanding, a frequentist interpretation should be something more like: we interpret the 90% as meaning that, of all patients with the same (or very similar) characteristics, approximately 90% of them would be expected to have heart disease.

So, why do we interpret the output of a frequentist logistic regression as a probability for a particular individual? Isn't that a Bayesian interpretation of probability?

I understand that there is also Bayesian logistic regression, where the parameters are estimated using Bayesian methods, but that is not what I am referring to here.

Could someone clarify where my reasoning is wrong?

items.title: references on semiparametric bootstrapping in mixed/multilevel models
items.body:
I'm having a hard time finding primary references on semiparametric bootstrapping (i.e. residual bootstrapping) for multilevel/mixed models. This CV question refers to Shang and Cavanaugh (2008), but that paper doesn't provide anything going further back. I can't find anything in Chernick (2011) or Efron and Tibshirani (1994) (I haven't looked at Davis and Hinckley, but I would be surprised if there was anything there ...) The other references listed below are interesting, but not useful as far as I can tell.

The basic question is how one should do residual-based bootstrapping for linear mixed models; do you resample both BLUPs/latent variables and residuals based on cluster-level residuals $\mathbf y - \mathbf X \hat{\boldsymbol \beta} - \mathbf Z \hat{\mathbf b}$ (Morris 2002 says this doesn't work)? Simulate $\mathbf b$ from the unconditional MVN distribution of latent variables (i.e., using the estimated random effects covariance matrices) and add those values to resampled cluster-level residuals and population-level predictions? Use resampled population-level residuals $\mathbf y - \mathbf X \hat{\boldsymbol \beta}$ added back to the population-level predictions?

The last option seems to be what's recommended, but I would really like to see the original discussion/theoretical justification for this ...

Chernick, Michael R. Bootstrap Methods: A Guide for Practitioners and Researchers. John Wiley & Sons, 2011.

Efron, Bradley, and R. J. Tibshirani. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. CRC Press, 1994.

Morris, Jeffrey S. “The BLUPs Are Not ‘Best’ When It Comes to Bootstrapping.” Statistics & Probability Letters 56, no. 4 (2002): 425–30. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0167-7152(02)00041-X.

Shang, Junfeng, and Joseph E. Cavanaugh. “An Assumption for the Development of Bootstrap Variants of the Akaike Information Criterion in Mixed Models.” Statistics & Probability Letters 78, no. 12 (2008): 1422–29. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spl.2007.12.015.

Thai, Hoai-Thu, France Mentré, Nicholas H. G. Holford, Christine Veyrat-Follet, and Emmanuelle Comets. “A Comparison of Bootstrap Approaches for Estimating Uncertainty of Parameters in Linear Mixed-Effects Models.” Pharmaceutical Statistics 12, no. 3 (2013): 129–40. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1561.

items.title: Causal Moderated Mediation Analysis to Explain a Null Result?
items.body:
Background

Bench scientists randomized genetically homogenous (or as homogenous as they can get) mice to exposure to a drug. Prior to their experiment, they constructed the following DAG

The drug has a direct effect on the outcome, as well as an indirect effect on the outcome via blood pressure.

After the experiment, the scientists note two important findings (summarized below in a plot):

  • Young Female mice saw a smaller treatment effect on blood pressure as compared to other strata, and
  • Young Female mice saw no treatment effect on the primary outcome.

Now, the bench scientists are seeking to answer why young female mice saw a null result. Were female mice protected from the outcome because they had a smaller blood pressure response, or because of something about being a young female mouse?

Question

I think a moderated mediation analysis should answer this, but it feels a bit strange to perform one on a null result. Given the total effect is equal to the sum the direct and indirect effects, I'm expecting to get estimates which are about equal in magnitude and opposite in sign for the young female strata.

Even if I did such an analysis, I'm not sure that would answer the bench scientist's question. That would simply tell me what the effect of the drug was through each of the pathway (assuming assumptions for the analysis are met, which I'm aware is a tall order already), not if the null result was because the blood pressure response was lower than other strata.

Does anyone understand what these scientists are asking me for and how I can give it to them or tell them it can not be answered?

items.title: Is it valid to compare two mean values when each mean is computed from a different number of datasets?
items.body:
I have two groups of datasets that all measure the same task:

  • Group A: 2 datasets

    Group B: 3 datasets

All of the datasets are of different sizes.

For each dataset I compute the same performance metric. Then I compute:

  • Mean_A = average of the metric over the 2 datasets

    Mean_B = average of the metric over the 3 datasets

Finally, I compute a reduction value:

Reduction = Mean_A – Mean_B

I need this reduction to prove a certain point in my problem I am working on.

However, my question is it statistically acceptable to compute a reduction value using two means that are averaged over different numbers of datasets (2 vs 3), as long as each dataset is treated as one unit?

Edit: This is a deep‑learning evaluation setup , where we are measuring how the performance of a deep learning model will drop when tested on new datasets that dont hold the same condiitons ( like same sensors) that exist in the data used to train the model. Each dataset is simply a collection of images used to compute one scalar performance metric ( how accurate the model predicted the disease in this image). There are no repeated measurements per subject; each dataset produces one metric value (the average performance over all images in that dataset).

The two groups differ only in how many datasets they contain:

Group A (2 datasets — “within‑conditions” - They are held out samples from the 2 datasets used for training the model) Dataset A1: 10 samples

Dataset A2: 15 samples

Group B (3 datasets — “shifted‑conditions”) Dataset B1: 155 samples

Dataset B2: 50 samples

Dataset B3: 50,000 samples ( for stress testing the model)

For each dataset, I compute the same metric (a single scalar for each image),then I average per dataset ( total number of images in the dataset) to get this metric for this dataset (metric A1, Metric A2) , then i get a mean value summarizing the performance on the "within conditions":

Mean_A = (metric_A1 + metric_A2) / 2

Same for the “shifted‑conditions” datasets:

Mean_B = (metric_B1 + metric_B2 + metric_B3) / 3

Then I measure the reduction as :

Reduction = Mean_A – Mean_B

So the question is specifically about whether is Reduction statistically acceptable to measure the drop in performance due to this shift in conditions given that it is comparing two means computed from different numbers of datasets, even though the datasets themselves have very different sample sizes, as long as each dataset is treated as one unit and they are all have the same task ( classifying a disease) ?

items.title: Intuition behind Tweedie's inverse distributions and waiting time
items.body:
One way to derive the inverse Gaussian distribution as a distribution for the first passage time ( Deriving Inverse Gaussian as First Passage Time of Wiener Process ) is to use the moment generating function.

Tweedie found out this relationship in diffusion problems or waiting time problems, where the distribution for a first transition can be described by the distribution for the diffusion/steps.

The moment generating function of the one distribution is the inverse of the other.

Can we give an intuitive motivation/explanation for this relationship?

I know that we can relate cumulative distribution functions in many of these type of problems. “The probability of taking time $t$ to hit $x$ is similar to the probability of being past $x$ at time $t$”. Like here: Limit distribution associated with counts (non-trivial combinatoric problem)

Since a long time I have suspected that this correspondence via cumulative distribution functions might be related to the inverse of the moment generating function. But I haven't gotten a good grasp of it yet.

Tweedie, Maurice CK. "Inverse statistical variates." Nature 155.3937 (1945): 453-453.

items.title: Fisher-Neyman fails for discrete distributions
items.body:
I'm reading Theory of Statistics by Mark J. Schervish, Section 2.1. After proving the usual Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem under the assumption that there is a $\sigma$-finite $\nu$ such that $P_\theta \ll \nu$ for all $\theta$, the author then states the following without proof:

Proposition 2.23. If $\{P_\theta: \theta \in \Omega\}$ is a parametric family such that each $P_\theta$ is a discrete distribution, then $T(X)$ is sufficient in the classical sense for $\Theta$ if and only if there are functions $m_1$ and $m_2$ such that $$\mathrm{Pr}(X = x | \Theta = \theta) = m_1(x)m_2(T(x), \theta), \text{ for all } \theta.$$ This proposition is needed only to handle cases in which $C = \bigcup_{\theta \in \Omega}\{x: P_\theta(x) > 0\}$ is an uncountable set; otherwise all $P_\theta$ are absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure on $C$.

However, it seems to fail trivially. A counterexample:

Let $(S, \mathcal{A}, \mu)$ be a probability space. Let $X: (S, \mathcal{A}) \to (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B})$, $T: (\mathcal{X}, \mathcal{B}) \to (\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{C})$ be measurable.

Let $\mathcal X=[0,1]$, $\mathcal B=\mathcal B([0,1])$. Let $\mathcal T=[0,1]$ with $$\mathcal C=\{A\subseteq[0,1]: A \text{ is countable or } A^c \text{ is countable}\}.$$ Then $\mathcal C$ contains all singletons. Define $$T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal T,\qquad T(x)=x.$$

For each $\theta\in[0,1]$, let $$P_\theta=\delta_\theta.$$ Then each $P_\theta$ is discrete, and $$P_\theta(\{x\})=1_{\{\theta\}}(x).$$ The factorization holds with $$m_1(x)=1,\qquad m_2(t,\theta)=1_{\{\theta\}}(t).$$

Now suppose $T$ were sufficient in the classical sense. Then there would be a kernel $r$ from $(\mathcal T,\mathcal C)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal B)$ such that, for every $\theta$, $r(\cdot,t)$ is a version of the conditional distribution of $X$ given $T=t$ under $P_\theta$.

Under $P_\theta=\delta_\theta$, $$T(X)=\theta\qquad P_\theta\text{-a.s.}$$ Hence the law of $T$ is $\delta_\theta$. Therefore the conditional distribution must satisfy $$r(A,\theta)=P_\theta(A)=1_A(\theta)$$ for every $\theta\in[0,1]$ and every $A\in\mathcal B$.

But a kernel requires $t\mapsto r(A,t)$ to be $\mathcal C$-measurable for every $A\in\mathcal B$.

Take $$A=[0,1/2].$$ Then $A\in\mathcal B$, but $A\notin\mathcal C$. Hence $t\mapsto 1_A(t)$ is not $\mathcal C$-measurable.

This contradicts the existence of such a kernel $r$. Therefore the factorization condition holds, but $T$ is not sufficient in the classical sense.

Anything I'm missing here?

items.title: Regression to the mean -- non normal example
items.body:
Let's agree that jointly distributed random variables $X,Y$ with the same marginals show regression to the mean iff for all $a > \mu$, we have $ \mu \le E(Y| X = a) < a$, with inequalities reversed if $a< \mu$, where $\mu$ is the common mean.

An example of this is given by $(X,Y)$ bivariate normal with the marginals having the same mean and standard deviation (non-zero) and correlation $\rho \neq \pm 1$. This follows from the fact that $E(Y|X) = \mu + \rho (X-\mu)$. My question is: are there examples that show regression to the mean other than the bivariate normal?

This would follow from the conditional expectation being linear in $X$, but I'm looking for a concrete example.

items.title: Interpreting random effect when random slopes are not modelled
items.body:
Background

Repeated-measures ANOVAs in psychological research treat the factor participant as a random factor. This treatment is desirable because participants represent one particular sample of the infinitely many samples that in principle could have been drawn from the population of interest. Including participant as a random effect thus ensures that observations from the measured sample generalise to the underlying population.

Two random factors, one fixed

I am interested in linear mixed models because they allow analysts to implement models with more than just one random factor as described by Judd et al. (2017)1. A second random factor could for instance be the specific items on which participants have been tested (stimuli, words, images...). Modelling both as random factors ensures that observations generalise both to other participants and to other items that could have been used in the experiment. The authors discuss several combinations for how random and fixed effects can be related to each other (such as crossed or nested) and provide code that implements these models in lmer. I identified the design that describes my application the best as the "CCC design", meaning that two random effects and the fixed effect that I am primarily interested in are fully crossed.

ccc_mod <- lmer(data = df, dv ~ ff + (ff|participant) + (ff|item) + 
                                (1|participant:item))

Problem: singular fits

In practice, however, when fitting this model to my data, R reports that I obtained a "singular fit". Based on the model output it appears that the by-participant slope has particularly low variance as well as the by-item slope (albeit slightly less so). The correlation between random intercepts and slopes are 1 or -1. Singular fits and correlations of -1 or 1 mean that the results should be treated with skepticism and it may be advisable to reduce model complexity until a model is found that does not produce such warnings (Brown, 2021). In my case, removing both random slopes (as well as the 1|participant:item random interaction term) results in a fit with diagnostics that appear fine, i.e., I receive no warning. In principle I am not too concerned that the "maximal model" may not be fully supported by the data and I can accept that model comparison is a normal part of linear mixed modelling practice (Matuschek et al., 2017), which all makes sense to me.

The one thing I am worried about is this: I would like to know what it means for the interpretation of the random effect item if I simply drop the random slope. Does this still allow me to make inferences from my observations that generalise to the broader population of items that could in principle have been included in my experiment although I am just modelling their intercepts as random?

Dataset and analysis details

In response to @PBulls's comment, I'm posting what my data for a participant look like because they asked about the number of replicates:

participant ff item dv
1 experimental A 3.14
1 control A 2.72
1 experimental B 1.24
1 control B 1.41
1 experimental C 1.62
1 control C 1.84
2 experimental A 9.81
... ... ... ...

The shown values for dv are fictional. This means that I have a single observation for each combination of factor levels, i.e., condition.

As shown in the table, there are only three levels for the item factor. Brown (2021, p. 4) recommends at least five levels for modelling item as a random factor. It seems I'm pushing the limits of LMMs. I analysed the effect of the fixed factor separately for each item and find that only two out of the three items yielded an effect of the fixed factor. (The average across items is significant btw.) This is why I am curious what to believe about the underlying population. Since the random slope (in my understanding) captures variability in the item-dependent sensitivity to the fixed factor manipulation, dropping it feels like the model is now inherently incapable of reflecting this heterogeneity; the intercept after all just enters into both levels of ff.

The dv are psychometric threshold estimates for three pairs of stimuli and each stimulus in a pair is matched to another one based on a particular image statistic.

items.title: “Paradox” with NHST
items.body:
Suppose we have a bag with only two balls. Each of the balls can be either black or white. We are interested to check whether the bag is a “fair” bag (with one black and white ball), and decide to perform Null Hypothesis Statistical Testing for that.

We repeatedly draw a ball out of the bag 10 times, returning the ball and shuffling after each draw.

Suppose that we got the sequence of colors:

WWWWBWWWWW

H0: p = 0.5

H1: p != 0.5

Under the H0, the probability of getting a result “as extreme” as the data is

2 * (10 * 0.5^9*0.5^1 + 1*0.5^10) = 0.02148438

Naively, we reject the null hypothesis.

However, thinking again, we realize that there is no possibility that a bag of only white balls would ever generate a black ball. Hence, the null hypothesis has to be true in this case.

We note that using the likelihood approach would have immediately given the correct and intuitive answer : with the sequence above, a mixed bag is the only option with likelihood larger than zero.

==================================================================

  • Does the above really show a problem with NHST?
  • If it is not a real problem, which step in the NHST procedure can prevent us coming to this wrong conclusion?
  • If it indeed is a simple paradox, then are there any realistic scenarios in which it could pose a practical problem?

items.title: Multiple regression when some predictors are identical across groups
items.body:
I am working on a multiple regression model examining the effects of several predictors on morphological traits to make interspecific comparisons across many species:

Length ~ Height + Average Weight + Diet Category

Firstly, because my data was collected from deceased specimens certain data was not obtainable specimen-by-specimen, including weight and individuals' diets. Secondly, because I am making interspecies comparisons, I find it acceptable to use species-wide/species average data in certain circumstances in lieu of specimen-level data. I have obtained average species weight and species diet category from published databases. (I am making the assumption that my data and the database data is representative of the population.)

My question is about the use of averaged data when it is identical for every observation (specimen) of the same group (species)...and this is the case for every group.

For example, this sample data where length and height are taken on a by-specimen basis but every specimen that's a part of species A has the same weight and diet category, and the same for species B and C:

Species Length Height Weight Diet Category
A 10 10 20 Carnivore
A 11 13 20 Carnivore
A 12 11 20 Carnivore
B 5 7 15 Herbivore
B 6 5 15 Herbivore
B 7 6 15 Herbivore
C 13 11 30 Omnivore
C 14 16 30 Omnivore
C 15 16 30 Omnivore

My initial thought to deal with this was to average length and height for each species so I would be comparing species averages to species averages and my unit of comparison is the species. However, it was recommended to me to look into using all my observations for higher statistical power (500 specimens instead of 40 species) and to avoid losing intraspecific variance.

I first looked into mixed modeling, but I found that this does seem to be an issue when you have a variable that is perfectly confounding with the grouping variable. In this case, I have up to 2+ perfectly confounding variables, depending on the model I'm running.

So I went back to regular regression. My findings seems to be that this kind of model is OK in multiple regression as long as there is 'enough' variation across the observations overall. However, I have struggled to find answers on this specific kind of problem where predictors are identical within every single group across every, or any way to judge what constitutes 'enough' variation. I understand that a single "average" variable is not too much of a concern because grouping is not part of the actual statistical analysis in regular regression like it is in mixed models, so I am especially concerned with what happens if there are multiple variables that are identical within groups.

items.title: Adjusting p values for multiple tests in R - ANCOVA with unequal slopes
items.body:
I have a dataset from testing different products that change bloom timing in trees. Outcome variable bloom day of year ("bd"), predictor variable "product" (a, b, c, d), continuous covariate "chill" (chill portions, a thermal time measurement of how much cold the trees experienced the winter prior to spring of bloom), with treatments randomly assigned to and sprayed on individual trees ("tree"). I've modeled it with an ANCOVA-like approach, though since the interaction violates the assumption of unequal slopes, I know it's not technically ANCOVA.

Through ANOVA, I've established that product, chill and the interaction of product:chill are significant. I want to know through post-hoc testing, how the products separate in terms of their impact to bd. I know that because of the interaction of product:chill, I should examine this at different chill accumulations.

I am struggling with how to adjust the p-value to account for comparing products at multiple levels of chill. Let's say I want to test at 3 levels of chill (46, 55, 65 CP).

Approach 1: If I test each level of chill one-at-a-time by using by =, as follows, I'm not adjusting my p-value for the tests of multiple levels of chill, just multiple products. Output tells me "P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 4 estimates".

Approach 2: The only other approach I've found searching online (that I've been able to understand) is to test all levels of product and chill at once, as follows. But this isn't a good approach either. Since chill is, on it's own, significant, I should already suspect bd of product-a at chill = 45 will be different from bd of product-a at chill = 65, for example. I just want to compare within levels of chill, not across.

What I want is something similar to Approach 1, with separate comparisons at each levels of chill, but with some accounting for the fact that I'm making three rounds of comparison.

Does such an approach exist? Suggested code for such an approach would be much appreciated.

Thanks very much in advance for your help, stackexchange universe!

library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
library(multcomp)

tree <- c(4, 18, 6, 20, 7, 21, 8, 22, 4, 18, 6, 20, 7, 21, 8, 22, 4, 18, 6, 20, 7, 21, 8, 22, 4, 18, 6, 20, 7, 21, 8, 22)
product <- c("a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "a", "d", "d", "d", "d", "d", "d", "d", "d", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "b", "b", "b", "b", "b", "b", "b", "b")
chill <- c(64, 65, 51, 63, 46, 56, 59, 50, 64, 65, 51, 63, 46, 56, 59, 50, 64, 65, 51, 63, 46, 56, 59, 50, 64, 65, 51, 63, 46, 56, 59, 50)
bd <- c(107, 108, 121, 110, 120, 120, 112, 124, 104, 104, 107, 102, 102, 104, 100, 108, 108, 113, 118, 106, 116, 118, 110, 114, 113, 113, 118,  106, 116, 118, 110, 120)
df <- data.frame(tree=tree, product=product, chill=chill, bd=bd)
df$tree <- factor(df$tree)
df$product <- factor(df$product)

model <- lmer(bd ~ product * chill + (1| tree), data = df)

emm_approach1 <- emmeans(model, c("product", "chill"), at = list(chill = c(46, 55, 65)))
cld(emm_approach1, by = "chill")

items.title: Error metrics for time series models when data has a small range

Near-zero values cause percentage errors to explode and distort the overall picture.

items.title: Unbiased estimator assumption for delta method
items.body:
The following is described as Univariate Delta Method:

Let $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ be a sequence of random variables such that $$\sqrt{n}(X_n - \mu) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2) $$ for some parameter $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$. Also let $g$ be a continuously differentiable function such that $g'(\mu)\neq 0$. Then $$\sqrt{n}\bigl(g(X_n)-g(\mu)\bigr) \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}\!\left(0,[g'(\mu)]^2 \sigma^2 \right). $$

My question is, to apply the Delta method, do we assume $\hat\mu = X_n$ is an unbiased estimator of $\mu$? If so, then why don't the statement of the delta method suppose so, or it's implicitly assumed? For instance, while proving the delta method, at some point, this proof says

We know by the WLLN that $\hat \mu \xrightarrow{p} \mu$.

But to use the weak law of large numbers, we need to assume $E[\hat \mu] = \mu,$ right? But did we really assume here?

Edit: I think in the proof, author's claim that "by the WLLN $\hat \mu \xrightarrow{p} \mu$" is not necessarily correct. I guess he is implicitly assuming that the estimator $X_n$ is a mean of some random variables $Y_n$. But even if he assume so, I think we cannot apply WLLN to conclude $\hat \mu = X_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu$ without assuming $E[Y_n] = \mu.$ But as pointed in the comment section, $\hat \mu = X_n \xrightarrow{p} \mu$ needs to be a consistent estimator of $\mu.$ But consistency of $\hat \mu$ already follows from the asymptotic normality of $\sqrt{n}(X_n - \mu)$.

items.title: When to calculate difference in proportion and when to do a repeated measures logistic regression
items.body:
I am collaborating on a paper where we are defining a binary outcome based on the number of criteria met by individuals on a psychological disorder checklist in DSM-5. There are 11 criteria in total that can be met by any one person.

In one version of the binary outcome a person had met criteria for the disorder if they meet 2 or more of the 11 criteria.

In the alternate version we removed two of the original 11 criteria, making a maximum possible count of 9. We once again define meeting criteria for the disorder as meeting 2 or more of the (now) nine criteria.

The lead author would like me to come up with a statistic stating the estimated difference in the proportion of people who meet the binary 'two or more' criteria based on the 11-item count and the proportion who meet the binary 'two or more' criteria based on the 9-item count, with a confidence interval of some kind.

My question is what would be the appropriate method to estimate the difference in proportion across the two different versions? My first instinct was a repeated measures logistic (specifically Bernoulli) regression with each participant getting a binary Yes/No for each version of the outcome. But then I wondered "is this really a repeated measures question?". It is not as if we measured the people twice. We simply have one version of an outcome and another version and want to compare the proportions across versions. Yet a simple test of difference in two proportions does not seem appropriate either since odds of meeting the binary criteria are not independent across the two different versions of the outcome.

Any advice much appreciated

items.title: Variance of plug-in estimator $\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})$ in Casella & Berger—numerical inconsistency?
items.body:
I am reading Statistical Inference by Casella and Berger and trying to understand the numerical values reported in Example 10.1.21.

Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be i.i.d. Bernoulli($p$), and the MLE of $p$ is $\hat p = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$ and consider the plug-in estimator $T = \hat p(1-\hat p)$

Since $Y=\sum X_i \sim \text{Bin}(n,p)$, the distribution of $T$ is discrete and its variance can be computed exactly by summation.For $n=24$ and $p=1/4$, I obtain $$ \operatorname{Var}[T]= \operatorname{Var}[\hat p(1-\hat p)]\approx 0.00191 $$ which is confirmed by simulation.

However, Casella and Berger report the value 0.00484 for this setting; I include a screenshot of the corresponding passage from the textbook below for reference.

My question is:

What exact quantity is being computed in the Table 10.1.1?

Is there an implicit rescaling or convention that I am missing, or could this be a numerical error in the text?

python code for simulating

import numpy as np
n = 24
p = 1/4
num_simulations = 10000000
data = np.random.binomial(1, p, size=(n, num_simulations))
Y = np.mean(data, axis=0)
T = Y * (1 - Y)
true_variance_simulated = np.var(T)
print(f"{true_variance_simulated:.8f}") ##output 0.00191022

items.title: Local interpretation of predictions from joint models for longitudinal and survival data

I am now trying to explicitly exploit longitudinal / time-series data, and I have started working with joint models for longitudinal and survival data. In particular, I am using the JMbayes2 package (mixed-effects models for the longitudinal part + Cox model for the event process).

items.title: Why do “good” loss functions in ML need both Lipschitz continuity and smoothness?
items.body:
I’m trying to understand the common assumptions in machine-learning optimization theory, where a “well-behaved” loss function is often required to be both L-Lipschitz and β-smooth (i.e., have β-Lipschitz gradients).

My confusion is the following:

If a function is L-Lipschitz, then the function value cannot change abruptly.

  • Doesn’t that already imply there are no “kinks” or “jumps” in the loss landscape? If so, why do we also need the β-smoothness assumption?
  • What exactly can go wrong if a loss is Lipschitz but not smooth?

In other words, what additional guarantee does β-smoothness provide that Lipschitz continuity alone does not?

If possible, I would appreciate concrete examples of functions that are L-Lipschitz but have gradients that behave “badly” (discontinuous, unstable, or wildly varying), and why such behavior causes problems for gradient-based optimization.

items.title: Use of differential equations in statistical modelling
items.body:
Consider a situation where there are multiple subjects and each subject has multiple measurements (response, covariates) over time. The goal is to identify a statistical regression model which allows past responses to influence future responses without creating statistical problems.

When the response is discrete, there are many modelling options for stochastic processes (discrete time and continuous time):

  • Multistate model regression for modelling the time based hazard of moving between State i and State j: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/49597683_Multi-State_Models_for_Panel_Data_The_msm_Package_for_R
  • Logistic regression for modelling odds of transitioning to State i given currently State j : https://hesim-dev.github.io/hesim/articles/mlogit.html

When the response is continuous, some choices include:

  • Time series models with exogenous variables
  • Dynamic Panel Models such as those based on the Arellano-Bond GMM estimator

But is it common to base a regression model on a Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE)?

For example, I found this interesting paper (https://gatesopenresearch.org/articles/4-71/v2) here where the authors seem to have adapted a SDE where the drift and diffusion components are themselves regression models.

Using SDEs seems to be the most natural approach as it directly models the response dynamics in continuous time/space as a function of changing response/covariates.

I would be interesting in reading more references on this and see how prevalent this is in statistics.

items.title: Does the CLT work in the opposite direction?
items.body:
The central limit theorem states that the sum of random independent variables of small effect approximates a normal distribution.

My question is: If I do observe a normal distribution, can I invoke the CLT and state that the distribution ought to originate from many variables of small effects (or from a single effect that is itself normally distributed)? And if I observe a markedly non-normal distribution, can I conclude that there must be one or few major effects standing out from a sea of small effects?

I surmise the answer is no to both questions. If so, are there any notable counter-examples from real life?

items.title: Why does my fixed effect model perform better than my random effect model?
items.body:
I've written a small simulation below to try and understand the differences in performance between fixed and random effects in a model.

I am imagining a bunch of eggs incubated together in a clutch (i.e., my observations within a given group). Half of the eggs in a clutch receive a treatment, and the other half do not (control).

library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)

set.seed(1772)

# Number of clutches
clutch_n <- 8
# Number of eggs per clutch
egg_n <- 50
# The IDs for each clutch and eggs, as well as Treatment name and global intercept
clutch_ids <- paste0("clutch_", 1:clutch_n)
egg_ids <- paste0("egg_", 1:egg_n)
treatments <- c("C", "T")
main_mean <- 60

# Make crossings
base <- crossing(clutch_ids, egg_ids) |>
  mutate(treatments = rep(treatments, length.out = n(), each = egg_n/2))
# Verify orthogonality
table(base$clutch_ids, base$treatments)

# Generate clutch random effects
clutch_effects <- rnorm(clutch_n, mean=0, sd=8)
names(clutch_effects) <- clutch_ids

# Generate responses
base <- base |>
  mutate(
    clutch_effect = clutch_effects[clutch_ids],
    treatment_effect = case_when(
      treatments == "C" ~ 0,
      treatments == "T" ~ -5,
    ),
    Y = main_mean + clutch_effect + treatment_effect + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.5)
  )

# Fixed effect model
m1 <- glmmTMB(Y ~ treatments + clutch_ids, base, family = gaussian())
summary(m1)
plot(simulateResiduals(m1))


# Random effect model
m2 <- glmmTMB(Y ~ treatments + (1|clutch_ids), base, family = gaussian())
summary(m2)
plot(simulateResiduals(m2))

Looking at the residuals, the model with random effects seems to be performing more poorly (S shaped residuals) than my fixed effect model. Why is that?

Some additional plotting:

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(base) +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = Y)) +
  facet_grid(clutch_ids~treatments)

items.title: Writing the profile likelihood in R
items.body:
Here is the log-likelihood of a two component normal mixture model:

$$\ell(\theta | x_1, ..., x_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log\left[ \pi \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_1^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x_i-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}\right) + (1-\pi) \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_2^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(x_i-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}\right) \right]$$

I want to use the profile likelihood (PL) approach to see how PL can be used to diagnose global and local identifiability. (Initially I thought that knowing if the Fisher Information Matrix is invertible or not is sufficient to determine identifiability, but it was explained to me here why this is not the case , i.e. FIM only describes likelihood surface at a very small region around the MLE and not the full surface Why is the profile likelihood used to determine if a model has a unique solution? )

Using R I simulated some data from a mixture model with pi = 0.3, mu1 = 0, mu2 = 5, sigma1 = 1 and sigma2 = 1.5:

x = c(3.75578358256322, -0.375602871669773, 4.13965959384758, -0.561876363549783,

Finally, for each of the 5 parameters, I made profile likelihoods plots:

    mle_pi <- fit$lambda[1]

    loglik_mixture <- function(pi, mu1, mu2, sigma1, sigma2, data) {
      n <- length(data)
      ll <- 0
      for (i in 1:n) {
        comp1 <- pi * dnorm(data[i], mu1, sigma1)
        comp2 <- (1 - pi) * dnorm(data[i], mu2, sigma2)
        ll <- ll + log(comp1 + comp2)
      }
      return(ll)
    }


profile_likelihood <- function(param_name, param_range, mle_values, data) {
  n_points <- length(param_range)
  profile_ll <- numeric(n_points)
  
  for (i in 1:n_points) {
    if (param_name == "pi") {
      fixed_pi <- param_range[i]
      obj_fun <- function(theta) {
        -loglik_mixture(fixed_pi, theta[1], theta[2], exp(theta[3]), exp(theta[4]), data)
      }
      start_vals <- c(mle_values$mu1, mle_values$mu2, log(mle_values$sigma1), log(mle_values$sigma2))
    } else if (param_name == "mu1") {
      fixed_mu1 <- param_range[i]
      obj_fun <- function(theta) {
        -loglik_mixture(theta[1], fixed_mu1, theta[2], exp(theta[3]), exp(theta[4]), data)
      }
      start_vals <- c(mle_values$pi, mle_values$mu2, log(mle_values$sigma1), log(mle_values$sigma2))
    } else if (param_name == "mu2") {
      fixed_mu2 <- param_range[i]
      obj_fun <- function(theta) {
        -loglik_mixture(theta[1], theta[2], fixed_mu2, exp(theta[3]), exp(theta[4]), data)
      }
      start_vals <- c(mle_values$pi, mle_values$mu1, log(mle_values$sigma1), log(mle_values$sigma2))
    } else if (param_name == "sigma1") {
      fixed_sigma1 <- param_range[i]
      obj_fun <- function(theta) {
        -loglik_mixture(theta[1], theta[2], theta[3], fixed_sigma1, exp(theta[4]), data)
      }
      start_vals <- c(mle_values$pi, mle_values$mu1, mle_values$mu2, log(mle_values$sigma2))
    } else if (param_name == "sigma2") {
      fixed_sigma2 <- param_range[i]
      obj_fun <- function(theta) {
        -loglik_mixture(theta[1], theta[2], theta[3], exp(theta[4]), fixed_sigma2, data)
      }
      start_vals <- c(mle_values$pi, mle_values$mu1, mle_values$mu2, log(mle_values$sigma1))
    }
    
    result <- try(optim(start_vals, obj_fun, method = "BFGS"), silent = TRUE)
    
    if (inherits(result, "try-error") || result$convergence != 0) {
      result <- try(optim(start_vals, obj_fun, method = "Nelder-Mead"), silent = TRUE)
    }
    
    if (!inherits(result, "try-error")) {
      profile_ll[i] <- -result$value
    } else {
      profile_ll[i] <- NA
    }
  }
  
  return(profile_ll)
}

pi_range <- seq(0.05, 0.95, length.out = 50)
mu1_range <- seq(-2, 3, length.out = 50)
mu2_range <- seq(3, 7, length.out = 50)
