items.title: Welch’s t-test and Kruskal-Wallis for small-sample water quality data with unequal variances and non-normality?
items.body:
We are testing a water filtration machine designed to clean lake water using one pump and two sequential filters. Our goals are:

To assess whether the machine effectively removes certain chemicals.

To identify whether each individual component (pump, filter 1, filter 2) affects chemical concentrations. (We suspect the pump itself might influence chemical levels.)

We collected water samples from four locations within the system:

  • Lake water (before the machine)

  • After the pump

  • After the first filter

  • After the second filter (fully treated water)

This schematic shows the sampling points:

We sampled on 9 dates, spread out over a season. On each date, we collected 1 sample per location (4 samples total).

The chemical concentrations in the lake fluctuate rapidly over time, and seasonal changes affect baseline levels. Due to this setup, we have no replicates per location per date, which limits our ability to separate the machine’s effects from natural fluctuations in the lake water.

Most chemicals passed the Shapiro-Wilk test for normality (p-values: 0.06–1). A few did not pass (p-values: 4.5e-6 to 0.04), and transformations (log, square root, cube root) did not help. Variance between locations is unequal, so standard ANOVA may not be suitable.

We propose the following methods to achieve both of our two goals:

Goal 1. Does the machine reduce chemical concentrations? We are comparing:

"Before the machine" samples (lake) vs. "After the machine" samples (after filter 2)

Test: Welch's t-test, which handles unequal variances.

Issue: Some chemicals are not normally distributed. Should we use a non-parametric test (like the Wilcoxon test) for those? Or use non-parametric tests for all chemicals for consistency, despite losing power?

Goal 2: Do individual components (pump, filter 1, filter 2) affect concentrations?

This requires comparing all four locations (lake, pump, filter 1, filter 2) like this: lake vs pump pump vs filter 1 filter 1 vs filter 2

test: Kruskal-Wallis test, because the variances are not equal, and I do not know an ANOVA test that allows for unequal variances.

Concern: Low statistical power due to small sample size (n = 9 dates), and even less power when using post-hoc tests to identify which components differ.

Would doing multiple welch t-tests be a better approach? Multiple testing does lower the power of a test, but are multiple parametrical tests less powerful than a non-parametrical Kruskal-Wallis test?

We use R to analyse the data

items.title: Spline and Log-transformation - are they mutually exclusive or not?
items.body:
Today I am dealing with a conceptual question.

Suppose I have a logistic regression model, with a binary response (dependent) variable, and a continuous predictor (say, age).

I want to analyse the relationship between age and the response variable and I want to use a logistic regression model. To do so, I want to account for the potential non-linearity of the association, so I would use restricted cubic spline to model age into the regression.

My questions are (partly based on some discussion I had with some colleagues):

  1. Is log-transformation of age (i.e., including log(age) in the model) an alternative to include age as a restriced cubic spline? [my guess is: no]
  2. Is there any reason why I should prefer to include log(age) instead of modelling age as a rcs?
  3. Can I combine the two approach, i.e. log transforming age, and then apply a spline to log(age)? If so, in which cases would this approach be appropriate? I were thinking of extremely skewed distribution of age
  4. Is there any case where including log(variable) is more correct than including variable as a restricted cubic spline?

My understanding of the question(s) is that restricted cubic splines (without log transformation) are always easier to interpret, from a graphical point of view, compared to the log() version of the same continuous variable, even if the shape of the curve may be smoother, as the former (rcs) would display the relationship between the actual variable with the response, while the log() transformed version of the variable would be much less easier to interpret - the only case in which log() may be easier may be when there are truly exponential relationship, but this is just my guess. Am I missing something?

items.title: Why isn't Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem (FWL) equivalent to fitting to residuals without orthogonalization?
items.body:
In the context of regression by iteratively fitting each predictor, why isn't FWL equivalent to fitting each predictor to the residuals of the previous predictor without orthogonalizing the predictors with respect to each other? In theory, each subsequent model should orthogonalize the predictor with respect to previous predictors by the fact that the collinear portion of previous predictors have been removed from the target.

In practice, results of obtained from the two methods differ.

items.title: Quantifying uncertainty after Friedman test with low sample size
items.body:
We are testing a water filtration machine that filters lake water using two sequential filters. The goal is to determine whether the machine effectively removes certain chemicals.

To test this, we collected three water samples each day for six days:

Unfiltered water (before entering the machine)

Once-filtered water (after the first filter)

Twice-filtered water (after the second filter)

Since the chemical concentrations in the lake vary daily, the samples collected on the same day should be treated as a group. This means we have six groups of three paired samples (one per day).

To determine whether the filtration process significantly changes the chemical concentrations, we performed a Friedman test. This test checks whether there are systematic differences between the unfiltered, once-filtered, and twice-filtered water across the six days.

As a result, we obtained a list of chemicals with their corresponding p-values, after correcting for multiple testing.

Since we only have six paired samples (n = 6 days), we expect a high risk of false negatives (Type II error): failing to detect a real effect.

This makes our results less reliable, and we need a way to quantify this uncertainty.

How to interpret our results given small sample size? A confidence interval would be useful, but our data does not follow a normal distribution (it contains multiple extreme values that are not true outliers).

Instead, we are considering estimating the minimum detectable difference—the smallest chemical concentration change that the Friedman test could reliably detect with 80% power at α = 0.05, given n = 6.

Is this possible? If so, how? Would it be possible to calculate this minimum detectable difference for each chemical, given our sample size and significance level? If so, how can we compute it?

R is used to analyse the data

items.title: What regression method should I use for non-normal, outlier-heavy biomedical data with a continuous outcome?
items.body:
I'm working with a large dataset of about 50,000 patients and trying to understand how protein expression levels influence erythrocyte (red blood cell) counts. The outcome variable — erythrocyte count — is continuous, measured in standard laboratory units. The predictors are protein expression levels, which come from a proteomics pipeline and are already log₂-transformed at the source.

The challenge is that none of the variables in my dataset are normally distributed, and both the predictors (3 proteins) and the outcome (erythrocyte counts) contain a large number of outliers. These outliers appear in every group — they are not limited to one extreme or one variable — and I believe many of them are biologically meaningful, not just noise. Because of this, I want to avoid filtering or transforming them in a way that would suppress their influence. These four boxplots illustrate the non-normal distributions and the presence of outliers in both protein expression and erythrocyte counts.

Following advice from a comment, I ran an OLS regression and examined the residuals (after log2 transforming the erythrocyte count ). The Q–Q plot shows clear deviation from normality, and the residuals-vs-fitted plot shows strong heteroscedasticity — the residual spread increases with fitted values: I also plotted the OLS regression line over the raw data for one of the proteins. The line appears to be pulled upward by a small number of extreme observations, confirming that the outliers have a visible influence on the model fit:

I know that OLS regression can technically still be used, but in my case, several assumptions are clearly violated like the heteroscedasticity for example. Because of this, I'm considering using quantile regression, specifically targeting the median (q = 0.5). It seems like a better fit since it's more robust to outliers and doesn’t rely on normality assumptions.

That said, I'm wondering: Is quantile regression at the median the best approach in this case, or would something like robust regression, GLMs, or a non-parametric method be more appropriate? My goal is to detect real associations without distorting or oversimplifying the data.

Also, would it be a good idea to group erythrocyte values (e.g., into low/normal/high ranges) and analyze them as categories — or would that introduce unnecessary bias or loss of information?

I’d really appreciate any guidance from people who’ve worked with large-scale clinical or proteomics datasets like this.

items.title: Evaluating a model in a small sample using a test set: bootstrap vs. LOOCV
items.body:
The thread Evaluating a classifier with small samples considers the problem in its title. Specifically, the question is about splitting off the test set from the rest of the data many times instead of just once to reduce variability of the estimate of out-of-sample performance.

Dave's answer suggests to follow Frank Harrell's advice. In Dave's words,

His recommendation for out-of-sample testing is to bootstrap the entire procedure by sampling with replacement from the entire data set, building the model on that new sample, evaluating model performance on the entire data set, and comparing this performance to the performance of a model trained and evaluated on the full data set. This is repeated dozens, hundreds, or thousands of times to get a distribution of performance differences. Again, his RMS book discusses this.

Another approach that seems intuitive to me in a small sample is (computational resources permitting!) to do nested leave-one-out cross validation (LOOCV). That is, in the outer loop, split off a single observation as the test set. Then in the inner loop do LOOCV to select and tune the model. LOO instead of K-fold should minimize the bias of the estimate of out-of-sample performance, something that may be quite important when dealing with small samples, as is the situation here. I suppose variance of LOO relative to, say, K-fold may or may not be a problem as per Bias and variance in leave-one-out vs K-fold cross validation (though that thread discusses simple instead of nested cross validation, so I am not sure to which extent it applies here).

cbeleites warns me in a comment to the first of the linked threads that this may not be a good idea. I am posting this here to figure out the details. Thus my question is, is Frank Harrell's approach preferable to mine and if so, what are the main drawbacks of my approach?

items.title: Experiment with sample sizes close to population - how to approach inference? (+FPC)
items.body:
this is a question I have thought about in the past but I can't convince myself of the correctness of the answer.

Let's say you are running a (true) experiment in all schools of a small country, and have a simple 2x2 experimental design. Let's also say you are interested in running a regression model on your entire dataset before the intervention. Finally, let's say I am not interested in generalizing my results to other countries - in theory, my "sample" equates to 100% of the population as it exists now. It is basically census data.

Now,when running an experiment I am dealing with two subgroups to which units have been allocated randomly, so I have two random subsamples. But should I apply a finite population correction here? I can't bring myself to believe that the population should be considered infinite, nor even one order of magnitude bigger than my sample. And how could I estimate the size of my population?

When working on my regression model, I would definitively be working with a sample with size close to ~90% of the population (assuming missing or unusable data). Using uncorrected classical inference would mean thinking of a greater population, which can only mean future+past schools. But would I want to do that? I could easily argue that my study cannot be generalized to 25 years in the future, as things could have changed enough to require a replication and reassessment.

So, what should I do? Thanks!

(variation: what if my data comes from every school, but for some reasons the experiment is ran only on 5% of their students?)

items.title: What law of probability is being used for deriving law of motion of distribution
items.body:
I'm studying this book and in page 788 (827 in the pdf page count) they show a law of motion for a joint probability distribution (image attached).

Basically, we have the following elements: a state space $A\times S=\{\bar{a}_1,\dots,\bar{a}_n\}\times\{\bar{s}_1,\dots,\bar{s}_n\},$ and there exists a decision rule $g:A\times S\to A$ which maps every state $(a,s)$ to an element $a'=g(a,s)$ in $A,$ that is to be interpreted as 'when the state today is $(a,s)$ the decision tomorrow is $a'$'. Additionally, there is a random variable $(s_t)_{t=0}^\infty$ with state space $S$ that has the Markov property with conditional transition probability $P(s_{t+1}=s'|s_t=s)$ given, where $s',s\in S$, and those probabilities are in the transition matrix $P$ mentioned in the text.

Then, the dynamics are as follows: we start with an initial state $(a_{0},s_{0})\in A\times S$, and then a sequence of realizations of the random variable $(s_t)_{t=1}^\infty$ induce a path for our system $(a_t,s_t)_{t=0}^\infty$.

Having said that, we are interested in the evolution of the joint unconditional distribution $\lambda_t(a,s):=P(a_t=a,s_t=s)$ of the state $(a,s)$ at any point $t$ in time. And thus we are given the formula that describes the law of motion of $\lambda_t$:

$$P(a_{t+1}=a',s_{t+1}=s')=\sum_{a_t\in A}\sum_{s_t\in S}P(a_{t+1}=a'|a_t=a,s_t=s)P(s_{t+1}=s'|s_t=s)P(a_{t}=a,s_t=s).$$

I'm capable of understanding this equation 'intuitively', but I have been unable to derive it formally using the laws of probability. Particularly, I have tried the law that allows us to write a joint probability in terms of conditional and marginal probabilities i.e. $P(X=x,Y=y)=P(X=x|Y=y)P(Y=y)=P(X=x|Y=y)\sum_xP(Y=y|X=x)P(X=x)$, but I don't see how I can transform this into the expression above.

I'd very appreciate if you could give me some insight into how to derive this equation.

items.title: Reconstructing count table when only pairwise features are visible
items.body:
Assume we are only able to observe two-way entry table counting the number of observations of a pair of categorical features $x_i,x_j$.

$$ \begin{array}{c|ccc} & & x_j & \\ \hline & & & \\ x_i & & y^{(ij)}_{ct} & \\ & & & \\ \end{array} $$.

We can sample all possible combinations of two features and all the tables refer to the same observations so that for each extraction $ij$ two elements of the table don't have to agree $y^{(ij)}_{ct}\neq y^{(kl)}_{ct} $ , but $\sum_{c,t} y^{(ij)}_{ct} = n$ for all $ij$ pairs. Effectively, the features partition the observed count.

I think that it is not possible to reconstruct a full count table as below (here $y_ct$ indicates the number of observations in country $c$ at time $t$ that shared a particular combination of categorical features listed on the right)

$$ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|} y_{ct} & c & t & x_1 &\ldots & x_i & \ldots & x_k \\ \hline & & & \\ & & & \\ & & & \\ \end{array} $$

since this would amount to reconstructing a joint distribution only knowing the marginals, which has multiple solution. What can we recover of the count table and with what consequences for inference (e.g. if we were to run a linear regression between y and the features)? Are there conditions on the data that allow full recoverability?

items.title: Separating interaction and main effects in generalized additive models
items.body:
I have previously asked about factor-smooth interactions for generalized additive models and received helpful answers: Smooth factor-interactions in generalized additive models

More generally I am interested the following type of model structure involving both smooth-factor and smooth-smooth interactions:

\begin{align} \text{log}(\mu) &= \underbrace{A_{0}}_{\text{intercept}} + \underbrace{f(x,y)}_{\text{main effect spatial smooth}} + \underbrace{\sum_{i}g_{i}(z_{i})}_{\text{main effects other smooths}} + \underbrace{\sum_{j} A_{j}}_{\text{main effects factors}} + \\ &\underbrace{\sum_{i}j_{i}(x,y,z_{i})}_{\text{smooth-smooth interaction}} + \underbrace{\sum_{j} h_{j}(x,y,A_{j})}_{\text{smooth-factor interaction}}, \end{align} i.e. spatial model at its core, which however also include the smooth and parametric effects of other covariates, and where these are allowed to interact with the spatial part.

My main question is: Is it possible to set up gam-models in mgcv, which with the correct set of identifiability constraints can meaningfuly isolate the different main and interaction effects in models of the type specified above?

Toy dataset To explore my question a bit further consider a specific example of (1), where there is only one other continous and categorial covariate: \begin{align*} &\text{Intercept}: A_{0} = 10 \\ \\ &\text{Main effect spatial smooth}: f(x,y) = \text{sin}(x)\text{cos}(y) \\ \\ &\text{Main effect other smooth}: g(z) = \text{exp}(-z/100)\cdot z/100 \\ \\ &\text{Main effect other factor}: A = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ if } A== a0 \\ 1 & \text{ if } A == a1 \\ 2 & \text{ if } A == a2 \end{cases} \\ \\ &\text{Smooth-factor interaction}: h(x,y,A) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{ if } A== a0 \\ \text{sin}(x)^2y & \text{ if } A == a1 \\ (xy)^{1/4} & \text{ if } A == a2 \end{cases} \\ &\text{Smooth-smooth interaction}: j(x,y,z) = (xy\cdot \text{exp}(-z/100))^{1/2} \end{align*}

To ensure identifiability I have chosen the first factor level $a0$ as reference. My question is then whether this along with apropriate boundary conditions for the continuous smooths in mgcv (effects should be zero at $x=0,y=0,z=0$) is enough to reproduce the following dataset generated with the specifications above:

N <- 11

data <- expand.grid(x = seq(0,1, length.out = N), y = seq(0,1, length.out = N), z = seq(0,1000, length.out = N), A = c("a0","a1","a2"))

intercept <- 10
value1 <- 1
value2 <- 2
eps <- 0.0


data <- data %>% mutate(intercept = intercept,
                        main_effect1 = sin(x)*cos(y),
                        main_effect2 = case_when(A == "a0" ~ 0, A == "a1" ~ value1, A == "a2" ~ value2),
                        main_effect3 = exp(-z/100)*z/100,
                        interaction1 = case_when(A == "a0" ~ 0, A == "a1" ~ sin(x)**2*y, A == "a2" ~ (x*y)**(1/4)),
                        interaction2 = (x*y*exp(-z/100))**(1/2),
                        epsilon = rnorm(nrow(data), sd = eps),
                        response_simulated = exp(intercept + main_effect1 + main_effect2 + main_effect3 + interaction1 + interaction2 + eps),
                        type = "simulated")

data$A <- as.factor(data$A)

Example without smooth-smooth interaction Let us first consider the case, where $j(x,y,z)=0$. In this case I use the following model-specification:

model <- mgcv::gam(response_simulated ~ s(x,y, pc = c(0,0), k = N*N-1) +
                                        s(z, pc = 0, k = N-1) +
                                        A +
                                        s(x, y, by = ordered(A), pc = c(0,0), k = N-1),
                   data = data,
                   family = gaussian(link = log),
                   method = "REML")

, which term by term produces the following plots:

predictions <- as.data.frame(predict.gam(model, data, type = "terms")) %>%
               rename(main_effect1 = `s(x,y)`,
                      main_effect2 = A,
                      main_effect3 = `s(z)`,
                      interaction_a1 = `s(x,y):ordered(A)a1`,
                      interaction_a2 = `s(x,y):ordered(A)a2`) %>%
               mutate(intercept = model$coefficients[[1]],
                  interaction1 = interaction_a1 + interaction_a2,
                  x = data$x,
                      y = data$y,
                  z = data$z,
                      A = data$A,
                      type = "fitted")




data_with_predictions <- bind_rows(data, predictions)


#plot intercept
plot1 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = x, y = intercept, color = type)) + ylim(0, 15) + geom_line()


#plot first main effect
plot2 <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y, fill = main_effect1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation main effect 1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot3 <- ggplot(predictions, aes(x, y, fill = main_effect1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted main effect 1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

#plot second main effect
plot4 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = A, y = main_effect2, color = type)) + geom_point()

#plot third main effect
plot5 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = z, y = main_effect3, color = type)) + geom_line()

#plot factor-smooth interaction for A="a1"
data_a1 <- data %>% filter(A == "a1")
predictions_a1 <- predictions %>% filter(A == "a1")

plot6 <- ggplot(data_a1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation interaction 1 a1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot7 <- ggplot(predictions_a1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted interaction 1 a1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

#plot factor-smooth interaction for A="a2"
data_a2 <- data %>% filter(A == "a2")
predictions_a2 <- predictions %>% filter(A == "a2")

plot8 <- ggplot(data_a2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation interaction 1 a2") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot9 <- ggplot(predictions_a2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted interaction 1 a2") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()



ggpubr::ggarrange(plot1, plot4, plot5, plot2, plot6, plot8, plot3, plot7, plot9)

Which almost perfectly reproduces the different terms in (1). I suspect the small deviations are due my model bordering on being unidentifiable. To ensure convergence I also had to use slightly less basis functions than the number of data points (i.e. k=N-1 in the model specification).

Example without smooth-smooth interaction Consider now the case, where the smooth-smooth interaction is turned on. As I want to separate interaction and main effects I use the ti()-specification for the smooth-smooth interaction. I furthermore use d=c(2,1) to exploit isotropy in $(x,y)$ but not with z, which is in another unit. This had led me to the following model specification:

model <- mgcv::gam(response_simulated ~ s(x,y, pc = c(0,0), k = N*N-1) + 
                                        s(z, pc = 0, k = N-1) + 
                                        A + s(x, y, by = ordered(A), pc = c(0,0), k = N*N-1) + 
                                        ti(x, y, z, d = c(2,1), k = N-1),
                   data = data,
                   family = gaussian(link = log),
                   method = "REML")

I suspect a more correct approach would be to set pc = c(0,0,0) in the ti(), but this is not possible due to a bug, which I have described in a previous post: Point constraints for mgcv smooths

Using the above model I get the following:

predictions <- as.data.frame(predict.gam(model, data, type = "terms")) %>%
               rename(main_effect1 = `s(x,y)`,
                      main_effect2 = A,
                      main_effect3 = `s(z)`,
                      interaction_a1 = `s(x,y):ordered(A)a1`,
                      interaction_a2 = `s(x,y):ordered(A)a2`,
                      interaction2 = `ti(x,y,z)`) %>%
               mutate(intercept = model$coefficients[[1]],
                  interaction1 = interaction_a1 + interaction_a2,
                  x = data$x,
                      y = data$y,
                  z = data$z,
                      A = data$A,
                      type = "fitted")




data_with_predictions <- bind_rows(data, predictions)

#plot intercept
plot1 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = x, y = intercept, color = type)) + ylim(0, 15) + geom_line()


#plot first main effect
plot2 <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y, fill = main_effect1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation main effect 1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot3 <- ggplot(predictions, aes(x, y, fill = main_effect1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted main effect 1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

#plot second main effect
plot4 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = A, y = main_effect2, color = type)) + geom_point()

#plot third main effect
plot5 <- ggplot(data_with_predictions, aes(x = z, y = main_effect3, color = type)) + geom_line()

#plot factor-smooth interaction for A="a1"
data_a1 <- data %>% filter(A == "a1")
predictions_a1 <- predictions %>% filter(A == "a1")

plot6 <- ggplot(data_a1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation interaction 1 a1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot7 <- ggplot(predictions_a1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted interaction 1 a1") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

#plot factor-smooth interaction for A="a2"
data_a2 <- data %>% filter(A == "a2")
predictions_a2 <- predictions %>% filter(A == "a2")

plot8 <- ggplot(data_a2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Simulation interaction 1 a2") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()

plot9 <- ggplot(predictions_a2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction1)) +
         geom_tile() +
         ggtitle("Fitted interaction 1 a2") +
         scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
         theme_void()


#plot smooth-smooth interaction for different values of z
data_z1 <- data %>% filter(z == min(z))
predictions_z1 <- predictions %>% filter(z == min(z))
z2 <- unique(data$z)[round(N/2)] #some number roughly in the middle of the interval
data_z2 <- predictions %>% filter(z == z2)
predictions_z2 <- predictions %>% filter(z == z2)
data_z3 <- data %>% filter(z == max(z))
predictions_z3 <- predictions %>% filter(z == max(z))

plot10 <- ggplot(data_z1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Simulation interaction 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

plot11 <- ggplot(predictions_z1, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Fitted interaction 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

plot12 <- ggplot(data_z2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Simulation interaction 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

plot13 <- ggplot(predictions_z2, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Fitted interaction 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

plot14 <- ggplot(data_z3, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Simulation interaction 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

plot15 <- ggplot(predictions_z3, aes(x, y, fill = interaction2)) +
          geom_tile() +
          ggtitle("Fitted main effect 2") +
          scico::scale_fill_scico(palette = "vik", na.value = "white") +
          theme_void()

ggpubr::ggarrange(plot1, plot4, plot5, plot2, plot6, plot8, plot3, plot7, plot9)
ggpubr::ggarrange(plot10, plot12, plot14, plot11, plot13, plot15)

Which also looks okay, but not as good as in the previous example. It seems like different terms now start to "mix".

Summary and questions So in conclusion and returning to the main question, the above analysis went some way in succesfully disentangling the different main and interaction effects for a very simple toy example. The separation was however not perfect, which leads me to the following question:

  1. For a more realistic dataset with a large number of other smooth covariates and factor variables can one expect to be able meaningfully separate main and interaction terms? Based on my toy example I could imagine that adding succesively more and more covariates would end up giving problems as I already saw in the example of adding the smooth-smooth interaction.
  2. The above conclusions of course assume that my model specifications are correct. Are they? And if so, are there better ways to achieve the separation I want? I am in particular interested in whether the use of the ti()-specification to separate out the interaction part is correct. I am also interested in whether the use of other basis for the smooths would achieve better results.

items.title: Variance or variation within sites and between sites
items.body:
I'm currently working on a large dataset of flux measurements from 29 lakes. Within each lake we have measured fluxes at 4-8 stations randomly spread out, with anywhere from 10-150 flux measurements at each station.

I want to find out whether flux measurements from one lake is more alike other measurements from the same lake, regardless of station, or if there is no difference between lakes.

My idea was initially to make a linear mixed model with random intercept, where I use station nested within lake in a null-model to see if the variance is higher for lake or the nested station:lake. However, I'm unsure if this really answers my question?

A small example of the code would be like below: A small note is that I have quite the extremes and a lot of 0 values, so I log transformed the flux values and added 1.

flux_df # df containing my flux measurements


m0 <- lmer(data = flux_df, log10(flux+1) ~ 1 + (1 | lake / station))

summary(m0)

Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method ['lmerModLmerTest']
Formula: log10(flux+1) ~ 1 + (1 | lake / station)
   Data: hourly_df

REML criterion at convergence: 33679.2

Scaled residuals: 
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.5343 -0.5326 -0.0235  0.5149  3.8362 

Random effects:
 Groups       Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 station:lake (Intercept) 0.3962   0.6295  
 lake         (Intercept) 0.4243   0.6514  
 Residual                 0.7584   0.8708  
Number of obs: 12932, groups:  station:lake, 130; lake, 29

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error      df t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   1.0159     0.1338 28.3822   7.591 2.62e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

From the summary output I see that the variance is almost equally for lake and station:lake, but I guess this still doesn't answer my question.

I looked into Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) which seems to explain the proportion of the variance that can be explained by the grouping. When

performance::icc(m0)

# Intraclass Correlation Coefficient

    Adjusted ICC: 0.520
  Unadjusted ICC: 0.520

The ICC is pretty much in between, so I guess this means that there are some effect of clustering the data, but not really that much? Or am I off here?

items.title: Bayesian estimation of a proportion taking into account complex sampling
items.body:
Here's my problem: I have a sample of 300 people from 3 different places (secondary data). I know approximately how people in the population of interest are allocated across each place (say 50% of people are in place A, 25% in place B, 25% in place C).

However, the sample does not reflect AT ALL this distribution (say it's 1/3, 1/3, 1/3, i.e. 100, 100, 100), because random sampling has been conducted at the "place level", not at the whole population level.

I want to get a Bayesian estimate of the proportion of women in the whole population across the three places (the proportion of women in each place is not really important to me). I have a beta prior for this proportion on the whole population, such as beta(a=5, b=2).

The data from the sample is a follow:

women men total
place A 57 43 100
place B 83 17 100
place C 48 52 100
Total 188 112 300

Usually, I'd simply do something like that in R:

library("bayesrules")
> plot_beta_binomial(
+     alpha      = 5,
+     beta       = 2,
+     y          = 188,
+     n          = 300,
+     prior      = TRUE,
+     likelihood = TRUE,
+     posterior  = TRUE
+ )

However I suspect this is very wrong, due to the fact the sample distribution across the different locations does not reflect well the real population.

Sampling was without replacement. Total population is about 5,000. This number is to relate to the approximate percentages above (that would be about 2500, 1250, and 1250, but I should probably put some prior on that as they are really approximations). I don't have much more details than that, unless I've missed something (I can try to request more info if needed, but unfortunately I have no guarantee I'll get an answer from people responsible for the sampling).

In this case, how to correctly estimate the proportion of women in the whole population?

Note that I mentioned the population size, but more generally I'd be interested in knowing how to handle things in case the population is much larger or much smaller (this could be useful for other studies on different populations).

Thanks.

(PS: I'm a beginner with Bayesian stats. Also, if it somehow matters, I tried asking this question to a LLM, before realizing that it could be well generating nonsense and I wouldn't know due to my ignorance on this issue, so I prefer asking it to human beings).

items.title: Checking a method for comparing vehicle encounters near arrivals and departures
items.body:
I’ve been recording encounters with a particular category of vehicle during everyday journeys. I’m examining whether these encounters are concentrated near departures and arrivals, after accounting for how much time I observe in those periods.

I have timestamped encounter records and journey start/end times. My comparison uses the first five minutes after departure and the last five minutes before arrival, counting overlapping windows only once.

I calculate:

Share of encounters within those windows ÷ share of observation time within those windows.

I’d appreciate feedback on whether this is a reasonable comparison and how to improve it. Routes, road conditions and times of day vary, and some vehicles travel together in groups. How should I account for those factors when assessing the apparent concentration?

Edit in -

Thank you. By “share” I mean a proportion:

  1. Encounter share: encounters with the chosen vehicle category inside the endpoint windows, divided by all recorded encounters with that category during the analysed journeys.

  2. Time share: observation minutes inside those windows, divided by total observation minutes during those same journeys.

The calculation I am asking about is encounter share ÷ time share, using the totals across journeys.

each endpoint window is five minutes. I combine the departure and arrival windows and count any overlap once. For example, for a fully observed 60-minute journey, the combined windows cover 10/60 of the observation time.

The analysis contains counts of encounters with the chosen vehicle category, without a comprehensive count of all passing traffic. Encounters do not necessarily represent distinct vehicles.

For scale, one dataset contains 20 journey legs lasting 8–89 minutes, with a median of 26.5 minutes, including legs with zero encounters. These are same-day journeys. A consistent distance range is not available in the prepared tables.

I would appreciate advice on whether this time-based comparison is useful and how varying traffic conditions and grouped encounters should be accounted for.

items.title: Stationary bootstrap for daily observations separated by market closures
items.body:
I am designing a historical trading-strategy study before calculating performance.

The proposed outcome is an equally weighted mean of daily net risk-normalized results. Complete eligible days with no trades contribute zero. Verified market closures are excluded; unexplained missing data blocks the analysis rather than being silently omitted.

Consequently, adjacent observations can be separated by different numbers of calendar days.

The proposed stationary bootstrap resamples consecutive observation indices using geometrically distributed block lengths and circular continuation. Expected block length is provisionally ceil(N^(1/3)); this is an unvalidated heuristic.

Under what assumptions is observation-index stationary bootstrapping appropriate for estimating uncertainty in this mean when calendar gaps vary? In particular, when would treating observations separated by a weekend as consecutive invalidate the dependence structure being resampled?

I am seeking methodological references or a counterexample, not an assessment of trading profitability.

items.title: Is it OK to train a logistic regression model with a binary predictor and then predict with proportional data?
items.body:
Is it OK to train a logistic regression model with a binary predictor and then use the fitted model predict over proportional data? Say I want to predict how tutoring affects exam results. In the training data the students either received tutoring or didn't (0/1) so I train the model like this (in R):

# Example data
data <- data.frame(
  received_tutoring = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  passed =            c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1)
)

# Fit logistic regression
model <- glm(
  passed ~ received_tutoring,
  data = data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(model)

But then I want to use the model to predict for students that only partially completed their tutoring (quantified as proportion of course completed):

# Make predict dataframe that includes proportions
new_data <- data.frame(received_tutoring = c(1, 0.5, 0.75, 0))

# Predict
predict(model, newdata = new_data, type = "response")

I appreciate this is not ideal but is it valid to approach it this way?

Edit:

Apologies, the above example is perhaps not the best. A better example would be one where the model is trained on a characteristic of individual students, e.g. male/female, but is then used to predict results at a broader scale, say for the whole class (i.e. proportion male/female):

# Example data
data <- data.frame(
  gender = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1),
  passed =            c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1)
)

# Fit logistic regression
model <- glm(
  passed ~ gender,
  data = data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(model)

# Make predict dataframe that includes proportions
new_data <- data.frame(gender = c(1, 0.5, 0.75, 0))

# Predict
predict(model, newdata = new_data, type = "response")

items.title: How can I separate the incremental predictive value of a delayed data source from the effect of waiting?
items.body:
I am designing a prospective observational study in which two data sources provide information about the same market events. The goal is to determine whether source B adds useful predictive information beyond source A, without confusing that contribution with the additional time required to receive B.

For each observation, I record the event timestamp, when my system received the information, when it became available for prediction, and its provenance.

Example

10:03 — Source A becomes available.

10:07 — Source B becomes available.

Source B may contain genuinely new information, duplicated information, or information caused by the same underlying event. Sometimes B never arrives.

I am considering two evaluations:

  1. Incremental predictive value

At 10:07, compare predictions using A alone against predictions using A+B, targeting the same future outcome and using only information available at that timestamp.

This would use paired predictions and a prespecified scoring rule.

  1. Operational value of waiting

Compare a policy that makes its decision at 10:03 using A with a policy that waits until 10:07 to incorporate B.

This would account for the later decision time, changes in the event's state, missing B observations, and opportunities that may no longer be actionable.

Both evaluations would use prospectively defined event cohorts and temporally separated testing.

My question

Is this two-part evaluation a statistically defensible way to separate incremental information from the cost of delayed availability? In particular, how should I handle selection bias when B arrives only for some events, and temporal dependence between observations?

I have reviewed discussions about incremental classifier evaluation and time-series cross-validation. They address sequential evaluation and temporal leakage, but not the distinction between the informational contribution of a delayed source and the value of waiting for it.

I would appreciate methodological references or guidance on an appropriate evaluation design.

AI disclosure: The title and body were drafted with assistance from OpenAI ChatGPT (GPT-6). I have personally reviewed the question before publication.

items.title: Kurtosis is a measure of dispersion?
items.body:
I propose that if you invert Pearson's kurtosis, you get a scale-free measure of dispersion that varies between $(0,1].$

$$ \kappa_\mathrm{invP}\left[ X \right] = \frac{\left( \mathbb{E}\left[ \left( X-\mu \right)^2 \right] \right)^2}{\mathbb{E}\left[ \left( X-\mu \right)^4 \right]} $$

Okay, then I compare it to the familiar scale-free measure of dispersion, the Coefficient of Variation $\sigma/\mu$.

Take two uniform distributions: $A=\{10,20,30,40,50\}$ each with equal probabilities; and $B=\{10,20,30,40,500\},$ again each with equal probabilities (the latter clearly has a Black Swan). From Distn A to Distn B, the CV goes from $0.4714$ to $1.5855,$ a clear increase in dispersion, which seems intuitive. My (inverse Pearson) measure goes down from $0.5882$ to $0.3090,$ which is not intuitive if you want to see it as a (scale-free) measure of dispersion.

CV has some problems as a measure: it's scale invariant but not translation invariant, it doesn't do negative values or a zero mean.

I've done a proof (via stochastic ordering) that inv-Pearson measures scale-free dispersion, but the results can seem upsetting. I'd love a fresh pair of eyes on this, what do you all think?

Disclosure: I'm the author of a preprint that develops this measure further, and it has some additional results beyond this. I'm asking here because I'd like the core idea picked apart by people who aren't me.

items.title: Finite sample approximation of the limit of a smooth function with uniformly distributed kinks
items.body:
Suppose that there is a probability distribution of kink-infested (nonsmooth) functions (forming a continuum with respect to some parameterization). Each of these functions has a set of independent variables (variables are not included in the parameterization). Across these nonsmooth functions, the position of the kinks varies: for any two of these nonsmooth functions, having coincident kink loci is a zero-measure coincidence condition that may get violated most of the time.

Suppose a set of nonsmooth functions are randomly sampled from the distribution of the nonsmooth functions. The mean of these sampled nonsmooth functions scales each kink on each sampled nonsmooth function by a factor in the range (0,1), which may cause the derivative-jump amplitude of each nonsmooth function's kinks to be expressed as "attenuated" in the landscape of mean expression.

Will this derivative-jump attenuation constitute an approximation of a smooth function, approaching that smooth function as sample size increases?

items.title: What criteria apply to unpublished studies included in a meta-analysis? (beyond eligibility)
items.body:
I am conducting a meta-analysis that includes both published studies and unpublished work — dissertations, theses, working papers and conference papers. The grey literature is searched systematically, and publication status is coded as a moderator.

Unpublished work has not been peer reviewed, which is sometimes taken to mean it warrants closer scrutiny. But applying stricter criteria to it risks reintroducing the selection effect that including grey literature is meant to counter.

Is there an established convention?

  • Do reviewers appraise published and unpublished studies against the same instrument, or add criteria for unpublished work?
  • Where the same instrument is used, is publication status handled solely as a moderator?

References to published methodological guidance would be more useful than opinion.

Any guidance is much appreciated! Best, Vicci

items.title: Should histogram bins be centred on rounded values rather than end at the sample maximum?
items.body:
I used this histogram tool with a custom bin width of 1, and I’m trying to understand how bin boundaries should be chosen for rounded measurements.

Consider a synthetic dataset containing 20 occurrences of each value:

0, 1, 2, 3, 4

There are 100 observations. With edges from 0 to 4, left-closed intervals, and a final interval that includes its upper endpoint, the frequencies are:

[0, 1): 20
[1, 2): 20
[2, 3): 20
[3, 4]: 40

The final bar has twice the height of the others, although each recorded value occurs equally often.

I understand that including the upper endpoint in the final bin is a documented convention, including in NumPy. The existing discussions on boundary conventions and equal-width binning explain endpoint choices and extending bins beyond the sample range.

My question concerns how the measurement process should affect this choice:

For measurements rounded to the nearest integer, is there a statistical justification for centring bins on the recorded values—for example, using edges at -0.5, 0.5, 1.5, and so on—rather than ending the histogram at the sample maximum?

Would that justification differ if the same values represented genuine counts rather than rounded continuous measurements?

My aim is to display the recorded distribution clearly, rather than estimate a population distribution from this synthetic example.

items.title: Are there established risk-of-bias instruments for correlational primary studies in a meta-analysis?
items.body:
I am conducting a meta-analysis of correlational field studies in organisational research. The effect size is a product-moment correlation between a predictor measured at the individual or team level and a performance, creativity or innovation outcome.

PRISMA 2020 requires a risk-of-bias assessment for each included study. Instruments I am aware of — Cochrane RoB 2, ROBINS-I, the JBI prevalence checklist, AXIS — were developed for trials or for prevalence and diagnostic studies, and their domains do not map onto correlational field research.

Is there an established instrument for appraising risk of bias in correlational primary studies contributing to a meta-analysis? Or is the convention for reviewers to declare a study-specific set of criteria?

For context, the criteria I have drafted are: construct validity of the predictor measure; reliability of all measures; justification of the rule used to combine sub-dimensions into a composite; common-method variance; alignment between level of measurement, aggregation and analysis; sampling frame and response rate; temporal separation between predictor and outcome; and selective reporting within the study. I rate each low / unclear / high rather than summing them.

Many thanks! Vicci

items.title: What is the best way to calculate game performance for a game that has adaptive difficulty over time?
items.body:
I’m working with a game where, for example, a player has to hit a moving ball with a racket. Every time they successfully hit the ball, the racket becomes smaller, making the next hit progressively more difficult. Once they miss, the racket resets to its original size.

Each round lasts 30 minutes, and I would like to compare performance across rounds.

I also have a chance/control condition where the racket doesn’t move, so some hits can happen simply by chance.

I would like to get a single normalized hit-rate/performance value for each round that tells me whether the player performed well or poorly overall.

Ideally, this value would take into account:

  • The racket getting smaller after each successful hit

  • The racket resetting after a miss

  • The fixed 30-minute duration

  • Different numbers of hits and misses across rounds

  • The chance-level performance from the stationary-racket condition

What would be the best way to calculate this as one normalized value? I’m particularly interested in something that accounts for the increasing difficulty as the racket gets smaller, rather than just calculating hits / total attempts. I have tried to calculate a score using the difference between the actual number of hits and the expected value of hits, but I think it does not take into account the paddle starting from where they last hit the ball (if it did not miss).

Also, if anyone knows of similar studies or experiments that have used a comparable normalized performance/hit-rate metric, I’d really appreciate any references or examples. Thank you.

items.title: Reporting Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in R: should I report W/V or another statistic?
items.body:
I'm writing up results from non-parametric tests in R and am a bit confused about the recommended reporting conventions.

For independent-group comparisons, I used wilcox.test() (Mann-Whitney U test). R reports a statistic labelled W. For paired-data comparisons, I also use wilcox.test() (Wilcoxon signed-rank test), where R reports a statistic V.

However, when reading papers and reporting guidelines, I've also seen different statistics reported: U (Mann-Whitney U) and W (Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic).

I currently write results as follows:

Wilcoxon signed-rank test: Condition A (median: __ , Q1-Q3 = __) showed a higher outcome X than Condition B (median: __, Q1-Q3 = __), V = __, p = __, r = __.

or

Mann-Whitney U Test: Group A (median: __ , Q1-Q3 = __) showed a higher outcome X than Group B , W = __, p = __, r = __.

My questions are:

  1. Is it statistically correct and sufficiently informative to report the W and V values produced by R directly?

  2. Is my way of writing up results clear and standard enough?

items.title: Likelihood Ratio Test for Uniform Parameter
items.body:
I am attempting to simulate the power function of a Likelihood Ratio Test where $X_1, \cdots,X_n\sim Unif(0,\theta)$ and the hypotheses are

$$H_0: \theta=\theta_0,H_1:\theta>\theta_0.$$

As far as I'm aware (corroborated by my computations), the unconstrained MLE is $X_{(n)}$, the sample maximum. I have obtained the following Likelihood Ratio Statistic:

$$\Lambda = \frac{1/\theta_0^n}{1/X^n_{(n)}}=\bigg(\frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta_0}\bigg)^n.$$

The rejection region for the LRT is, from what I understand, $R=\{\Lambda<c\}$. Thus I found that $c=\alpha$ and $\beta(\theta^*)$, the probability of rejecting $H_0$ when $\theta=\theta^*$ is

$$P\bigg\{\bigg(\frac{X_{(n)}}{\theta_0}\bigg)^n<\alpha\bigg|\theta=\theta^*\bigg\}=\bigg(\frac{\theta_0}{\theta^*}\bigg)^n\alpha.$$

The issue that I'm currently facing is that, when I simulate the power curve, the power decreases as I move farther into $\Theta_1$. This seems to run counter to how a power curve should behave, but this oddity seems to be corroborated by the above power function.

I'm not sure if I made a mistake in my computations. If not, why does this occur?

items.title: Delta method + synthetic control
items.body:
I have a causal inference task but I'm not sure which method is appropriate. The crux is that I have multiple regions and multiple regions where treatment exists when $region=r; time \ge t$ for some specific $r, t$. This seems to be exactly aligned with synthetic control! But my use case involves a ratio metric, specifically a percentage (successes out of trials.) Outside of the world of synthetic control (SC), I'm aware of the "delta method" where OLS can be used on a ratio metric. The core idea is:

  1. Pool over all subgroups as the pooled success rate, $ r = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N s_i}{\sum_{i=1}^N k_i}$
  2. For any given unit, extract the expected successes under r as $\hat{s_i} = r \cdot k_i$
  3. regress $\Delta_{s_i} = s_i - \hat{s_i}$ on the treatment exposure

If the treatment explains the variation in $\Delta_s$ then you've inferred change in success rate attributable to treatment exposure.

great! But for SC, some questions.

  1. Is SC used to model success rate directly, the trials or the successes?
  2. Assuming SC estimates the trials counterfactual, $\hat{k_i}$ such that the $r \cdot \hat{k_i}$ is the effect size, is $r$ pooled pre-event or over full timeline?

items.title: Pooling adverse-event proportions across trials when registries only report events above a threshold: is this estimator and interval defensible?
items.body:
I'm summarising how often a given adverse event (e.g. nausea) is reported for one drug across many clinical trials, using only the per-arm adverse-event tables posted to ClinicalTrials.gov. The goal is a descriptive cross-trial summary per drug and event, not a treatment effect versus placebo.

Current estimator:

  1. Each arm gives a proportion $p_{ij}$ (trial $i$, arm $j$) with its number at risk $n_{ij}$.
  2. Arms within a trial collapse to one entry: the unweighted mean of that trial's arm proportions.
  3. Trial entries are pooled with weights proportional to sample size (times an extraction-confidence factor between 0 and 1).
  4. The 95% interval is built on the log-odds scale and adds a between-trial heterogeneity term to the sampling variance, then is back-transformed.
  5. A cell with fewer than 3 distinct trials reports nothing.

Two features of the data worry me:

  • Reporting threshold. Registries list non-serious adverse events only when they exceed a per-trial threshold (usually 5% of an arm). A trial where the event occurred below that threshold posts no row and simply drops out, so for low-frequency events the observed trials are a selected, high-rate subset.
  • Heterogeneous trials. Each cell mixes populations (obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular-outcome trials), doses and follow-up lengths; rates are as posted, not annualised. Very large trials can carry most of the weight.

Questions:

  1. Is sample-size weighting with an added between-trial variance a reasonable estimator here, or would a standard random-effects model on logit proportions (e.g. GLMM / binomial-normal) be clearly better for this descriptive purpose?
  2. Is collapsing arms to an unweighted within-trial mean defensible, or should arms enter as clustered observations?
  3. Is there a practical way to adjust for the reporting threshold (treating unreported trials as left-censored below 5%, for example), or is disclosure plus a minimum-trial floor the honest limit?
  4. Given the population mix, is it better to report one pooled figure with the interval widened by heterogeneity, or only stratified figures?

Code for the estimator (TypeScript, Apache-2.0): https://github.com/saurabhgoyal75/magistra-predictor/blob/main/methodology/side-effects-engine.ts (function pooledClinicalEstimate). Full method write-up: https://github.com/saurabhgoyal75/magistra-predictor/blob/main/preprint/magistra-methodology.md (sections 2.3, 2.5, 4).

items.title: Interpreting Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition with sector dummy variables — negative explained component
items.body:
I'm running a Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition on a binary outcome (high-earner status within a sector, 0/1, split at the sample median) using the oaxaca package in R. My call:

oaxaca_highearner <- oaxaca(high_earner ~ educ_level + n_children_u5 + n_elderly + urban | female,
                             data = as.data.frame(sector_sample))
summary(oaxaca_highearner)

Group A (male, n=8,268) mean = 0.5106; Group B (female, n=1,918) mean = 0.4426; raw gap = 0.0680.

The threefold decomposition gives:

Endowments (explained): -0.0329 (-48.4% of the gap)
Coefficients (unexplained): 0.0969 (142.4%)
Interaction: 0.0041 (6.0%)

The negative explained component comes from women in my sample having higher average education (10.78 years) than men (10.41 years) within this subsample.

I independently ran a Fairlie-style decomposition (manual, using separate glm(family=binomial) models for each group, predicting one group's outcome using the other group's fitted coefficients) on the same outcome and variables, and got a similar pattern: explained = -0.0346 (-50.8%), unexplained = 0.1026 (150.9%).

My question: is a negative explained component with magnitude larger than the total gap (so the unexplained component exceeds 100% of the gap) a statistically valid and interpretable result, or is this a sign I've misspecified something — e.g., is it inappropriate to use the oaxaca package (designed for continuous/OLS outcomes) on a 0/1 outcome at all, even as a linear-probability-model robustness check alongside a proper logit-based Fairlie decomposition? Is there a cleaner or more standard way to report/verify this specific pattern (negative endowments, overshooting unexplained component)?

items.title: How good is AUROC for prediction models?
items.body: The area under the ROC curve is based on sensitivity and specificity. In the context of prediction P(Disease|Test), Sen and Sp are retrospective P(Test|Disease). Thus, AUROC is NOT a good measure of the PREDICTIVE performance of a model. It is good for discrimination of the known outcome but not for prediction of the yet unknown outcome. Please see https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12470336/. Am I correct? Full reference Indrayan A, Mishra S. Assessing the Adequacy of a Prediction Model. Indian J Community Med. 2025 Sep-Oct;50(5):739-744. doi: 10.4103/ijcm.ijcm_567_24. Epub 2025 Mar 31. PMID: 41017898; PMCID: PMC12470336.

items.title: How to properly supply soft evidence to a Bayesian netwerk model in R (gRain, bnlearn)
items.body:
Let's suppose we have some Bayesian network model based on the bnlearn::learning.test dataset:

library(gRain)
library(bnlearn)
library(Rgraphviz)

bfit <- bn.fit(hc(learning.test), learning.test)
graphviz.chart(bfit)

My goal is that I want to be able to ask the question: if the marginal density of node $A$ was different, say $(0.8, 0.1, 0.1)$, how would that change the marginal density of $E$?

It is my understanding that this is a form of soft evidence. I am looking into using the gRain package to do exactly this, but I am unsure if I'm using the right tools.

From the gRain documentation I learned that I can supply soft evidence via:

bfit_grain_evidence <- bfit |> 
  as.grain() |> 
  evidence_add(evidence = list(A = c(0.8, 0.1, 0.1)))

and I can see that there is a change in marginal density for node $E$:

querygrain(as.grain(bfit), nodes = "E") 
# marginal in original network: 
# E
#         a         b         c 
# 0.3886140 0.2977371 0.3136489 

querygrain(bfit_evidence, nodes = "E")
# marginal in network with soft evidence on A:
# E
#         a         b         c 
# 0.4977566 0.2955325 0.2067108

My issue is: I am not sure that I did what I wanted to do. When I try to querygrain the marginal for $A$ in the network with soft evidence, it returns a NULL value:

> querygrain(bfit_evidence, nodes = "A")
NULL

Moreover, I've read that there are multiple meanings of the term "soft evidence", and I am not sure that gRain is using the definition that I'm interested in. See, e.g., this paper.

So my questions are:

  1. is the code above doing what I want it to do?
  2. if not, how should I do it in R?

items.title: Is this two-state absorbing Markov chain a valid model of failure risk across N stages with stage-dependent error rates?
items.body:
Hypothetical setup. A process has $N$ sequential stages, each running $n$ independent steps. A stage's input is clean or contaminated. Per-step deviation probability is $p$ for clean input and $r=\min(1,pc)$ for contaminated input ($c\ge1$). A deviation is severe with probability $q$; a severe event ends the process and counts as a failure. A stage with at least one non-severe deviation hands on contaminated output with probability $g$.

Define, for clean and contaminated input respectively:

$$a_C=(1-p)^n,\quad s_C=(1-pq)^n,\quad u=s_C-a_C$$

$$a_D=(1-r)^n,\quad s_D=(1-rq)^n,\quad v=s_D-a_D$$

Here $a$ is the probability of no deviation, $s$ is the probability of no severe event, and $u,v$ are the probabilities of at least one deviation but none severe. I write one stage as

$$ M=\begin{pmatrix} a_C+u(1-g) & a_D+v(1-g)\\ u\,g & v\,g \end{pmatrix} $$

(columns = current state, rows = next state), so that

$$ P(\text{at least one severe event})=1-\mathbf 1^{T}M^{N}e_1,\quad e_1=(1,0)^T . $$

Example: $p=0.4,\ q=0.5,\ c=5,\ g=1,\ n=3,\ N=2$ gives $0.852408$, versus $0.737856$ if all steps were independent. I checked the arithmetic in code and in Wolfram Alpha, and with $c=1$ or $g=0$ it matches the independent result.

Question: Is $M$ a correct way to represent this process, so that $\mathbf 1^{T}M^{N}e_1$ is exactly the survival probability? If not, what is wrong with the setup?

items.title: Model selection: discrete-time survival, piecewise exponential, or Andersen-Gill for a time-varying exposure within repeated observation intervals
items.body:
I have person-interval data in discrete, mostly contiguous, protocol-driven time intervals. Interval dates are standardized across person with a fixed length with slight variation driven by protocol. The target of our analyses is within-interval occurrences, but most individual persons contribute multiple intervals over time.

Our variables are Event X and Event Y. Within each person-interval, we know whether or not Event X and Event Y each occurred, and on exactly what date(s). Event X is effectively a time-varying covariate within the interval, and Event Y censors the observation for the remainder of the interval. We are interested in the first instance of Event X within the interval (once Event X=1, then Event X=1 for the remainder of the interval). In practice, Event X can occur before or after Event Y within an interval, but only an Event X that occurs before the first Event Y is considered causally relevant, and the remainder of the interval should be censored after the first occurrence of Event Y.

Our research question is: "Does Event X prevent Event Y, within intervals?"

More exactly: "Does the first instance of Event X in a person-interval where Event Y has not yet occurred reduce the risk of a future first occurrence of Event Y within that person-interval?"

Each person-interval is only at risk until their first instance of Event Y, after which their remaining person-interval time should be censored. They will re-enter the risk set during the start of the next interval and can again experience Event X and/or Event Y. Persons are nested within a higher order grouping variable, so I will need a multi-level/mixed model.

I have honed in on these approaches as possible options:

  1. Multi-level Discrete-Time Survival model - GLMM with binomial distribution and cloglog or logit link, with dataset expanded to person-day structure
  2. Piecewise Exponential model for survival data - GLMM with Poisson distribution and log link, person-interval data structure with Offset for interval length reflecting censoring
  3. Andersen-Gill extension of Cox Proportional Hazards or a broader Counting Process model - start stop intervals, exact dates, would use frailty/random effects

Can anyone offer any feedback regarding selecting a model? I am interested in any sort of feedback, and especially interested in comparing how primary results are interpreted and correctly articulated (in general, and for translatability to non-technical staff). I can use SAS or R.

Thank you

items.title: Estimating remaining time to sustained recovery with repeated daily landmarks within stock drawdowns
items.body:
I am designing an exploratory study of Egyptian stocks, initially ABUK and FWRY. At the close of each session during a drawdown, the intended prediction is the remaining time until a sustained recovery, conditional on information already available. This is not a request for a stock recommendation.

A provisional recovery label is the first close above the maximum of the previous 10 closes, followed by 5 closes above that pre-breakout level. Those future 5 closes label the outcome; they must not enter prediction features. The label is a working choice, not an established definition of a market bottom. Administrative end of observation and missing/unusable follow-up must not be silently counted as recoveries or losses.

I want to screen one predictor at a time (e.g. 3-session return or current volume divided by the preceding 20-session mean), then evaluate incremental predictive value jointly. Multiple daily prediction origins belong to one drawdown, multiple drawdowns belong to one stock, and stocks share market shocks.

Real preliminary data audit, not model results: stock,observed_dates,provisional_consistent,provisional_single_source,unresolved ABUK,6057,523,4761,773 FWRY,1577,516,450,611

These dates cover 2000-01-12 to 2026-02-04 for ABUK and 2019-08-07 to 2026-02-04 for FWRY. Source overlap is deduplicated by stock and date. Prices that disagree are unresolved rather than averaged. Corporate-action and calendar reconciliation remain unfinished, so these are not counts of usable independent events.

For the dependence created by repeated daily landmarks within the same drawdown, what risk-set construction and validation unit are appropriate for estimating calibrated probabilities of recovery within 5, 21 and 126 sessions? In particular, is a discrete-time landmark survival model appropriate, and how should episode-level dependence be handled when comparing individual predictors? I would retain whole episodes within chronological folds and remove training outcomes that overlap test periods; I am seeking criticism of this design before fitting.

Disclosure: ChatGPT assisted with drafting this question and running the exploratory data audit. The study objective comes from the researcher; the audit is not independent validation or evidence of predictability.

1. Binomial GLMM

I first ran a binomial model with the glmmtmb package in R. My y variable was modeled as a binomial outcome that represented the number of beetle damaged seeds per plot. My fixed effects were plant_trait_a and plant_trait_b and I set planting_block as a random effect.

Using the DHARMa package I checked the residuals plots then tested for overdispersion and zero-inflation. I found that there was significant overdispersion (dispersion = 1.9633, p-value < 2.2e-16) and zero-inflation (ratioObsSim = 8.2305, p-value < 2.2e-16).

library(tidyverse)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)

set.seed(42)
beetle<-glmmTMB(cbind(seeds_beetle_damaged, seeds_total-seeds_beetle_damaged) ~ plant_trait_a*plant_trait_b + (1|planting_block),

plot(residbeetle)
#left plot or QQ plot residuals was S shaped
#right plot looked ok: Levene test for homogeneity of variance was n.s. and within group deviation from uniformity was n.s.

#check dispersion and zero inflation
testDispersion(residbeetle) 
#dispersion = 1.9633, p-value < 2.2e-16, significant overdispersion
#see plot, red line is far to the right of predicted values

testZeroInflation(residbeetle)
#ratioObsSim = 8.2305, p-value < 2.2e-16, significant zero inflation

2. Zero-inflated beta binomial

Next I ran a zero-inflated beta binomial model using the same fixed and random effects. I read online that the beta binomial distribution can address overdispersion in binomial models. Compared to the binomial model, the left side residuals plot (QQ plot) looked better - no longer S-shaped, data points were closer to red diagonal line. The p-value from the dispersion test was nonsignificant (dispersion = 1.3461, p-value = 0.096).

beetle2<-glmmTMB(cbind(seeds_beetle_damaged, seeds_total-seeds_beetle_damaged) ~ plant_trait_a*plant_trait_b + (1|planting_block),
                 family=betabinomial, ziformula = ~ 1, data=seeddamage)

# AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
#    391.6     406.1    -188.8     377.6        52 

residbeetle2<-simulateResiduals(fittedModel=beetle2)
plot(residbeetle2)
#both residuals plots look good

#check dispersion and zero inflation
testDispersion(residbeetle2)  # Tests for over/underdispersion
#dispersion = 1.3461, p-value = 0.096

3.Zero-inflated beta

I shared the results from the zero-inflated beta binomal model with a stats consultant at my university who uses SAS and has mostly worked with binomial GLMs. He said he's only seen one textbook mention the beta binomial distribution, and that since it's not as common as other distributions he is skeptical of the results.

So I decided to try running a model with a zero-inflated beta distribution. This seems somewhat more common than the beta binomial. I used the same fixed and random effects, but the y variable was changed to the proportion of beetle damaged seeds per sample (prop_beetle_damaged). The residuals plots looked good and the dispersion value was nonsignificant (dispersion = 1.3836, p-value = 0.056)

beetle3<-glmmTMB(prop_beetle_damaged ~ plant_trait_a*plant_trait_b + (1|planting_block),
                 family=beta_family(), ziformula = ~ 1, data=seeddamage)
summary(beetle3)
# AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
#    -75.6     -61.1      44.8     -89.6        52 

residbeetle3<-simulateResiduals(fittedModel=beetle3)
plot(residbeetle3)
#residuals plots look good

#check dispersion and zero inflation
testDispersion(residbeetle3)  # Tests for over/underdispersion
#dispersion = 1.3836, p-value = 0.056

Which model seems most appropriate for my data? I've read that when deciding between models with different distributions, the one with the lowest AIC value is the best fit. So should I go with the zero-inflated beta model?

items.title: Is the statistical formula given in the text previously known or not?
items.body:
I have never found this formula anywhere, although it has a very simple idea behind it. It is also useful and not nonsense.

$$ r_R = \frac{6\frac{\sum XY}{\sum Y} - 3(N+1)}{N-1} $$

It measures growth rate (related to the highest polynomial degree exponent) of the non-negative values Y against the corresponding values of X, which in the formula are forced to behave like indices, so X values are 1,2,...

If the Y-values are also restricted to be the same as the X-values but shuffled in any permutation order, the formula actually gives the Pearson correlation between X and Y values. That is how I first used the formula, and due to its history as being first used for rank correlation, I call it Ranta correlation.

When the (Y)-values are freed to be any non-negative values, the name “correlation” starts to sound strange, because the formula then measures non-linear relationships and its range becomes [-3, 3].

Polynomial examples

Let us test some polynomials of different degrees, using the sequences from Pascal’s triangle. Because of how the formula behaves, we need only the first two values of each sequence (although you may use more if you want, the result will be the same).

0th degree polynomial: 1, 1
1st degree polynomial: 1, 2
2nd degree polynomial: 1, 3
3rd degree polynomial: 1, 4
4th degree polynomial: 1, 5
5th degree polynomial: 1, 6
6th degree polynomial: 1, 7

And what the Ranta correlation formula gives:

0th degree polynomial: 0
1st degree polynomial: 1
2nd degree polynomial: 3/2
3rd degree polynomial: 5/3
4th degree polynomial: 7/4
5th degree polynomial: 9/5
6th degree polynomial: 11/6

This produces a very regular rational sequence.

Converting Ranta correlation to a polynomial exponent

There is a simple inversion formula:

$$ \text{exponent} = \frac{2\, r_R}{3 - r_R} $$

This is generalization from the observation polynomes. The exponent needs not be an integer. For example, if Ranta correlation = 0.6, then

$$ \frac{2\cdot 0.6}{3 - 0.6} = 0.5, $$

which corresponds to a square-root type growth.

Any growth of Y-values that is Big O(X^2) (not just the Pascal polynomial of degree 2) will give a Ranta correlation approaching 3/2 as the number of points goes to infinity. In practical statistics, 30 points may be enough to estimate the exponent.

Sorting algorithms inspired by the formula

The basic idea behind Ranta correlation is that sum(XY)/sum(Y) is maximized by ordering the Y-values in ascending order. This leads to two sorting algorithms:

Ranta correlation sort:
Each round, compare all index pairs and swap the pair that gains the largest positive surplus in iY_j + jY_i compared to the original iY_i + jY_j.
Very efficient swaps, but expensive due to large number of multiplications and comparisons.

Snailsort:
Each round, compare all index pairs and swap the pair that gains the smallest positive surplus.
Probably the sorting algorithm with the largest number of swaps, but with guaranteed progress at every swap.

items.title: How to statistically prove the uniqueness of a composite feature vector formed by concatenating multiple distinct categorical embeddings?
items.body:
I am working on an entity resolution problem where each individual is represented by a composite vector formed by concatenating learned embeddings from several distinct domains:

$$ X_i = \left[ E_A(H_{i,A}) \;\middle\|\; E_B(H_{i,B}) \;\middle\|\; E_C(H_{i,C}) \right]. $$

Each $E_k$ is a dense, continuous embedding produced by a domain-specific model (e.g. BERT or another sequence model) and represents a different aspect of the individual's longitudinal history.

My intuition is that the combination of these histories could act as a kind of individual fingerprint: even if a single domain is not sufficiently distinctive, their combination may be highly specific to an individual.

I would like to understand how this intuition can be formalized mathematically.

  1. Can it be proven, or at least bounded probabilistically, that the composite feature vector is unique (or sufficiently unlikely to be shared) between two distinct individuals?
  2. What assumptions about the underlying data or the embedding functions would be necessary to make such a statement?
  3. Are there established mathematical or statistical frameworks for analyzing the uniqueness or discriminative capacity of such a composite representation?

items.title: Application of Mahalanobis distance in experimental design
items.body:
Attached is latex for a question that I have. I have also attached a background, if you wish to only read the question go to the second section.

Let's say we are in perfect OLS world where we have all of our typical assumptions:

$$Y=X\beta+\epsilon$$

$$X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times p};R\in \mathbb{R}^{q\times p}$$

$$(X^TX)^{-1} \ \text{exist}$$

$$E(\epsilon \ | \ X)=0$$

$$\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon \ | \ X)=\sigma^2I_n$$

$$\epsilon \ | \ X \sim N(0,\sigma^2I_n)$$

Define a hypothesis test as

$$H0: R\beta-r=0$$

$$Ha:R\beta-r=\delta$$

Let $D^2=(R\hat\beta-r)^T(\operatorname{Var}(R\hat\beta-r))^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)=(R\hat\beta-r)^T(\sigma^2R(X^TX)^{-1}R^T)^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)\sim\chi^2_{\text{rank}(R)=q}$.

Let us represent modifications of $D^2$ as simply $\mathcal{D}$, for standardized distance. This is in reference to how if you instead take $\hat D(s)^2=(R\hat\beta-r)^T(s^2R(X^TX)^{-1}(R\hat\beta-r)=D^2(\frac{\sigma^2}{s^2})\sim \chi^2_q(n-q)/\chi^2_q.$ Then, since we know this looks a lot like the $F$ distribution, we can simply modify $\hat D(s)^2/q\sim F_{q,n-p}$. I wish to say that there are many other examples of canonical $\mathcal{D}$'s out there but I will not write them all.

Since we now have a general way to talk about our sense of distance I wish to discuss errors in this context.

$$\alpha=P(\mathcal{D}\in R \ | \ R\beta-r=0)$$

$$\beta=P(\mathcal{D}\notin R \ | \ R\beta-r=\delta)$$

One can imagine a spherical $\mathcal{D}$-length neighborhood around the origin, representing our data acquired (cloud-q); a spherical $c$-length neighborhood around the origin, representing our null (cloud-w); and a spherical $c$-length neighborhood around the point $e=\operatorname{Var}(R \hat \beta-r)^{-1/2}\delta$, representing our alternative (cloud-e).

From the above we can make geometric definitions of type I and II errors by relating the area overlapped by the $c$-length spheres and our $\mathcal{D}$-length sphere. Type I error is the fraction of cloud-w falls outside of cloud-q. Type II is the fraction of the cloud-e that falls inside of cloud-q.

$$\textbf{Type I} \sim w-q:w$$

$$\textbf{Type II} \sim e\cap q:q$$

Note that the distance from the origin of cloud-e, simply $e^Te=\lambda$, is related to or the general case for quite a few important concepts: Cohen's d, signal-to-noise ratio but square it, effect sizes, etc.

Actual Question

I have a question about the following object:

$$\lambda(\delta)=\delta^T(\operatorname{Var}(R\hat \beta-r))^{-1}\delta.$$

$$\max_X \lambda(\delta)=\max_X\delta^T(R(X^TX)^{-1}R^T)^{-1}\delta$$

Do you know of anything/anyone that deals with this object? It feels very important to me seeing how you could use some simple optimization of it to gain higher power results in testing. It also, I believe, would be very influential in picking the "optimal" experimental design.
